articles.title: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?  Al JazeeraU.S. President wants 60 days to analyse impact of Russia sanctions law, says Marco Rubio  The Hindu‘India diversified imports, but hard to pivot in one day’: Marco Rubio explains why US waived some Russia energy tariffs  Hindustan TimesPause on Trump’s punitive tariffs gives India relief, but trade uncertainty persists  Telegraph IndiaChristmas cheer, but caution remains:...
articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”.
Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027.
Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour.
Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort.
While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas.
Here’s what we know:
Which sanctions has Trump waived?
In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.
The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month, named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia.
They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil.
The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order.
US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”.
Who will benefit from this?
Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted.
He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”.
Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”.
Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties.
While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain.
Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices.
According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards.
“If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency.
Which countries still buy oil from Russia?
China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank.
Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added.
Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore.
Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m).
Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia?
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.
But despite its own near-blanket ban on Russian oil, the EU has continued to import large quantities of Russian gas, though it plans to phase out those imports next year.
Urgewald, a Germany-based group that researches coal companies, reported this week that more than 12 million tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG was transported into EU ports from January to September this year, a 9.5 percent jump from the same period last year.
In September, EU countries imported 817 million euros ($918m) of pipeline gas, and 615 million euros ($691m) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to CREA.
EU members France and the Netherlands were the largest LNG importers, bringing in 446 million euros ($501m) and 116 million euros ($130m) respectively, according to the think tank. France’s LNG imports represented a 103 percent increase from the previous month, it added.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron has been among the most outspoken about Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying on Friday that it “sends a negative message” and would have no impact on global prices.
Hungary imported the most Russian pipeline gas of any EU member by far during the month, with 414 million euros ($465m) worth. Slovakia and Bulgaria brought in 161 million euros ($181m) and 132 million euros ($148m), respectively, according to CREA data.

articles.title: India’s goods trade deficit widens - Business Recorder
articles.summary: India’s goods trade deficit widens  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India’s merchandise trade deficit widened to USD30.21 billion in September as the rise in imports outpaced that in exports, though a rise in outbound shipments and trade deals could narrow the balance over coming months.
The trade gap has widened as Asia’s third-largest economy grapples with a prolonged Iran war that has made energy costlier, hurt shipments to the Middle East and battered markets.
India raised interest rates earlier this month and announced a raft of measures to support the rupee. India’s trade deficit stood at USD26.86 billion in August.
Merchandise exports rose to USD44.40 billion in September from USD43.81 billion in the previous month, while imports increased to USD74.61 billion from USD70.67 billion. Export growth was broad-based, reflecting strength across sectors including petroleum products, meat, dairy, poultry, electronic goods, handicrafts, and engineering goods, Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters.
India is seeking to diversify its export markets, with a trade deal with New Zealand set to take effect next week and its pact with the UK already in force, while a broader agreement with the EU is moving towards implementation.
Agrawal said negotiations with the US were moving in the “right direction,” with legal work underway. “We anticipate concluding and signing the trade deal at the earliest possible time,” Agrawal said, adding that India was seeking preferential market access and greater tariff stability under the proposed agreement.
Ties with the US have been rocky this past year over issues including President Donald Trump’s repeated claim of brokering an India-Pakistan ceasefire and a US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers.
The US remained the top destination for Indian exports, with goods shipments rising to USD50.81 billion in April-September from USD45.82 billion a year earlier.
India’s services exports stood at USD36.35 billion in September, and imports at USD19.44 billion, trade ministry estimates showed. Overall goods and services exports rose 13.84 percent year-on-year to USD476.20 billion in April-September from a year earlier, while imports increased 15.68 percent to USD551.13 billion, data showed.

articles.title: US tariff waiver on Russian crude a comforting relief, but trade uncertainties persist: CareEdge Chief Economist Rajani Sinha - India's News.Net
articles.summary: US tariff waiver on Russian crude a comforting relief, but trade uncertainties persist: CareEdge Chief Economist Rajani Sinha  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 17(ANI): In the high-stakes arena of global energy politics, Washington's decision to pull back on its aggressive tariff threats has handed India crucial macroeconomic breathing room, according Rajani Sinha.
Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, told ANI on Saturday that while the tariff waiver provides comforting relief, India must remain cautious amid uncertainties in global trade dynamics.
Addressing the threat of steep US tariffs, Sinha noted that markets viewed the rhetoric primarily as a negotiating technique rather than an immediate structural threat.
'Up to 100% tariff that the US had threatened India with, we were not much concerned about it,' Sinha said. 'We viewed that more as a negotiating technique by the US'.
However, she cautioned that the reprieve might be temporary, underscoring the importance of securing a comprehensive bilateral trade deal with Washington.
Sinha highlighted that the waiver benefits the United States just as much as its trading partners, given Washington's own energy security concerns and widening diesel crack spreads.
With global oil markets remaining volatile, she pointed out that India's refined petroleum products are vital for helping the US curb domestic inflation.
On the energy front, Sinha noted that while Russia has become a critical source supplying over 30 per cent of India's crude imports, the historical discounting advantage has significantly narrowed.
Russian crude currently trades at around $117 per barrel compared to Brent spot prices near $120.
'The benefit that India enjoyed in terms of lower Russian oil, that has really, I would say, dwindled,' Sinha remarked, adding that Russian imports now serve primarily to secure steady, reliable energy availability rather than steep price discounts.
Despite high crude prices, India's macroeconomic buffers remain resilient.
Sinha projected the current account deficit (CAD) to stay comfortably between 0.8 per cent and 1.2 per cent of GDP, supported by robust double-digit growth in merchandise and services exports.
Headline inflation is expected to average around 5 per cent for the fiscal year, though persistent crude prices above $100 per barrel could pose upside risks if passed on to consumers.
On the currency front, she attributed recent rupee depreciation primarily to adverse global sentiment and foreign capital flows rather than weak domestic fundamentals.
Turning to the fiscal deficit, Sinha noted that healthy direct and indirect tax collections will provide a substantial cushion.
Concluding with the government's disinvestment pipeline, she addressed market debates regarding the IDBI Bank stake sale.
Backing the move, Sinha stressed that the transaction represents a positive step toward meeting budgetary targets and reducing the state's footprint in the commercial sector.
'I do not see any concern for the banking sector,' Sinha affirmed, noting that India's banking health and robust NPA metrics remain well-positioned.
The move comes after US President Donald Trump waived the sanctions provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which could have imposed tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, including India and China. Trump invoked Section 115 of the Act, citing US national interests, amid a diesel supply deal with Russia.
India had conveyed its concerns to Washington over the legislation, with the Ministry of External Affairs on Wednesday, reiterating New Delhi's position that stability in global energy markets must be maintained. (ANI)

articles.title: Non-tariff barriers biggest hurdle in India-China trade: Sitharaman - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: Non-tariff barriers biggest hurdle in India-China trade: Sitharaman  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
China’s restrictions on Indian exports have emerged as the biggest obstacle to bilateral trade, widening India’s trade deficit despite an improvement in diplomatic relations between the two countries in recent times, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Friday.
During her interaction with the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, Sitharaman flagged China’s extensive use of non-tariff barriers, which she said had prevented Indian exporters from accessing the Chinese market despite significant opportunities.
“I would think a decade has gone, consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products. But non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly, whether it is in the name of phytosanitary measures or any other for which due investigations can happen. Both sides can resolve the issues by talks. But no progress has been made. So, non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China,” the minister said.
India has recently relaxed Press Note 3 norms, which had restricted Chinese entities from making foreign direct investment in India through the automatic route. However, the widening trade gap remains a key concern, with imports from China continuing to far exceed exports.
According to the latest government data, India’s imports from China rose nearly 28% to $80.35 billion during April-September this year, while exports stood at $11.41 billion.
India’s trade deficit with China more than doubled to $112 billion in FY26 from $52.7 billion in FY16.
“The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking with China now for several years; we are denied market access even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China,” Sitharaman said.
She said the two countries could address concerns over non-tariff measures through dialogue and investigations, but there had been little progress. New Delhi, meanwhile, had refrained from imposing retaliatory non-tariff restrictions or countervailing duties on Chinese goods.
On the India-US trade negotiations, Sitharaman expressed hope that the agreement would be concluded soon.
“I hope in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners India and US the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest,” she said.

articles.title: Non-Tariff Barriers Biggest Hurdle in India-China Trade: Nirmala Sitharaman - Open Magazine
articles.summary: Non-Tariff Barriers Biggest Hurdle in India-China Trade: Nirmala Sitharaman  Open Magazine
articles.full_text:
Non-tariff barriers remain the biggest obstacle to trade between India and China, with restricted market access for Indian goods contributing to a widening trade imbalance, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Friday.
Speaking at an interactive session with Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council on India’s Economic Edge, held on the sidelines of the World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Sitharaman said India had repeatedly raised concerns over the barriers faced by its products in the Chinese market but had seen limited progress.
“So non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China,” she said, adding that the trade imbalance continued to grow despite years of engagement between the two countries.
Sitharaman said Indian products faced restrictions even in sectors where the country was globally competitive and where demand in China offered significant opportunities.
“We are global leaders in generic drugs, bovine meat, vegetables and perishables and very many such goods which have huge potential in China,” she said.
She alleged that China used measures such as phytosanitary requirements to restrict market access, arguing that these issues could be addressed through investigations and bilateral discussions.
INDIA FAVOURS DIALOGUE OVER RETALIATORY TARIFFS
Sitharaman said India had chosen to pursue discussions rather than respond to trade barriers with countervailing duties or similar restrictions.
She contrasted India's approach with that of countries that impose tariffs to address what they consider unsustainable trade imbalances.
“That approach we have never taken,” she said, adding that negotiations could be slow but remained India's preferred way of resolving trade disputes.
The remarks highlight a longstanding challenge in India-China economic relations: despite substantial bilateral commerce, the trade balance is heavily tilted towards China. India has repeatedly sought greater access for its exports while raising concerns about dependence on Chinese imports.
Non-tariff barriers include regulatory requirements, product standards, licensing procedures and other restrictions that can affect the movement of goods across borders, even when tariffs are not the principal obstacle.
INDIA-US TRADE AGREEMENT ALSO IN FOCUS
Beyond China, Sitharaman expressed hope that India and the United States would conclude their proposed trade agreement at the earliest opportunity.
She referred to recent remarks by India's commerce minister indicating that both sides wanted to move towards signing the agreement soon.
“I hope, in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners, India and US, the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest,” she said.
India has been pursuing trade agreements with several partners as part of its efforts to expand export opportunities, improve market access and diversify economic relationships.
Sitharaman reiterated India's commitment to multilateralism while highlighting its trade engagements with the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Canada and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, alongside negotiations with the US.
Her comments come as governments worldwide reassess trade relationships amid tariff disputes, supply-chain concerns and efforts to secure more favourable terms for domestic industries.

articles.title: Zelenskyy hints at potential meeting with Putin in US during G20 summit as Trump waives Russian Oil tariffs - India's News.Net
articles.summary: Zelenskyy hints at potential meeting with Putin in US during G20 summit as Trump waives Russian Oil tariffs  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
Kyiv [Ukraine], October 18 (ANI): Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday said that a potential trilateral meeting involving Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place in the United States during the upcoming G20 Summit in December, adding that confirmation from Moscow and Washington was still awaited.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy said the United States was actively involved in negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, stressing that pressure should be increased on Moscow rather than Kyiv.
He expressed readiness to participate in peace talks 'anywhere' and 'in any format', adding that the American side had indicated that a meeting could take place 'next week.'
'The American negotiating track will continue. We're counting on them to put more pressure on Putin, not on us. Otherwise, it's simply unfair. As for our meetings with the American side - we expect to meet and are ready to meet in Ukraine or in Europe. If they want to meet in America, let them invite us. We're ready to negotiate anywhere, and we're ready for any format: three-way, two-way, four-way, five-plus - it doesn't matter. What matters is peace. The American side has given us a signal that our meeting with them can happen next week,' he stated.
Zelenskyy added that Washington had also proposed a trilateral meeting involving Russia and Ukraine, with potential venues including the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia, another European country or the United States during the upcoming G20 Summit.
He said that confirmation from Russia or the US is impending.
'Regarding a meeting with Putin, the United States is working on this. They have a proposal for a trilateral meeting. This meeting can take place in one of the Middle Eastern countries. The United States has always mentioned the UAE or Saudi Arabia. Another possibility is for the meeting to take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from Russia or from the United States. The meeting could also take place in one of the European countries. I know that the Europeans are starting contacts about this. We'll see how things turn out a little later,' he noted.
Furthermore, Zelenskyy suggested that European countries pursue their own path for negotiations with Russia. On that note, he expressed willingness to hold talks with Turkish President Erdogan about sea and food security among representatives of Middle Eastern countries.
'And, of course, in my view, Europeans need to have their own infrastructure and their own track for negotiations with Russia. We need to pursue every possible avenue to stop the war. We'll also speak separately with Trkiye. I plan to talk separately with President Erdoan about the sea and food security, and with representatives of Middle Eastern countries,' the Ukrainian President added.
In a separate post, Zelenskyy expressed disappointment over US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil as part of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously waiving several sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.
Reflecting on the recently announced diesel deal between the US and Russia, the Ukrainian leader asserted that the sanctions relief will unfortunately continue.
He claimed that Trump's latest decisions, relieving pressure from Russia amid the ongoing conflict, are a major defeat to late Senator Lindsey Graham, who Zelenskyy highlighted 'pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible.'
'Sanctions relief will continue. I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately. It's unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey. He devoted his life to America. We had an excellent relationship with him. And shortly before the tragedy, Lindsey was in Ukraine. He always supported us very strongly and pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible,' he wrote.
Calling Trump's decision to undo the bill, which garnered bipartisan support from Republicans and Democrats alike, Zelenskyy said, affirmed that it will not stop the war, but instead fuel Russian satisfaction.
'It's difficult without him, I'll be honest. I want to thank both Democrats and Republicans who supported his bill. That was a major victory: this truly bipartisan support. And now, the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me. And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people. This certainly does not stop the war,' the Ukrainian leader noted.
Trump has waived several sanctions related to Russian fuel sales that were to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a month after signing the Bill.
The legislation would have authorised tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.
The decision comes amid a reported diesel supply agreement with Russia, as fuel prices in the United States remain a concern ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorises the President to waive the application of sanctions provisions against foreign persons, restrictions on persons and duties imposed under the law.
'I have submitted to Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act,' Trump said in the order.
He also waived the application of duties under Sections 112 and 113 of the Act. These provisions authorised the President to increase duties on goods imported into the United States from Russia to as much as 500 per cent ad valorem, or relative to the value of the goods. They also provided for duties of up to 100 per cent ad valorem on goods from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas.
The development follows Trump's announcement of a diesel supply agreement with Russia, under which he said Moscow would immediately supply more than 3,00,000 tonnes of diesel fuel, followed by another 5,00,000 tonnes during November and one million tonnes immediately thereafter.
Simultaneously, Trump said he wanted the Russia-Ukraine war to end, claiming that both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wanted an end to the conflict.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said, 'Well, you know, I know the details, okay? And at some point, I'll release the details. But I don't care anything except for one. I want that war ended. 25,000 soldiers on average a month are being killed. Last month, it was 32,000 soldiers. And I think the two leaders, I deal with both of them. I think they want that war ended, too, and I think it's going to end. That's all I care about. I want that war to end.'
Meanwhile, Putin praised Russian military strikes against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities and logistics centres, according to Russia's state-run TASS news agency. He ruled out discussing the establishment of a security zone along Russia's border territories during potential peace negotiations with Ukraine. (ANI)

articles.title: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure - Devdiscourse
articles.summary: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure  Devdiscourse
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy.
US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy. Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously waiving several sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.
The order provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18, but suspends their application through a presidential waiver. "Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the White House Executive Order stated.
The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn, while existing Russia-related sanctions under other Executive Orders remain unaffected. According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), the decision provides India temporary relief but leaves open the possibility of Washington restoring tariff pressure during future trade negotiations.
In its report titled "U.S. Waives Russian-Oil Tariffs: Temporary Relief for India, but Uncertainty Remains," GTRI said, "For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty." R Ramachandran, former Director (Refineries) at Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), told ANI that the immediate benefit for Indian oil companies would be greater crude sourcing flexibility rather than necessarily higher refining margins.
"So more than the GRM, what actually impact it will have on Indian refineries will be the availability of more crude choices," he said. Gross refining margin (GRM) refers to the difference between the value of petroleum products produced by a refinery and the cost of crude oil processed.
Ramachandran explained that increased Russian crude availability could help refiners secure more economical supplies, depending on discounts. However, lower crude prices could also be accompanied by falling petroleum product prices, limiting gains in refining margins. Rajani Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, said Russia's importance to India has increasingly shifted from discounted oil towards ensuring uninterrupted supplies.
"The discount has really reduced significantly. But yes, what is more important for India now is availability and ensuring consistent supply of crude oil for the economy," Sinha told ANI. She said Russia's share of India's crude imports had exceeded 30 per cent in recent years, although its price advantage over international benchmarks had narrowed.
GTRI noted that Russia's share in India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as purchases shifted towards the United States and the United Arab Emirates. The think tank also highlighted Washington's own energy requirements as a possible factor behind the waiver.
According to its report, the United States agreed to purchase Russian diesel under an October 9 agreement to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices. It also noted that Washington had agreed not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that targeting India alone could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations.
"The message is clear: U.S. interests determine when penalties apply, while the ability to retaliate helps secure protection," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said in the report. Meanwhile, Ramachandran said a sustained waiver could help reduce freight costs and ease logistical constraints associated with Russian oil shipments.
He said greater vessel availability and smoother payment arrangements could improve crude procurement economics. "If Russia and India can agree upon on a continued ruble-rupee exchange for this, it also supports to ease the foreign exchange outgo which currently is affecting the Indian Rupee's strength," he said.
However, these benefits would depend on the restrictions that remain applicable. On the broader economic impact, Sinha said India's current account deficit could remain manageable despite elevated crude prices, supported by merchandise and services exports.
She expects the current account deficit to remain between 0.8 and 1.2 per cent of GDP, assuming crude prices range between USD 80 and USD 100 per barrel during the remaining financial year. However, persistently higher prices could widen the deficit towards 1.5 per cent of GDP under adverse conditions.
Sinha expects average inflation of around 5 to 5.5 per cent, although higher fuel costs and food inflation remain risks. She said the fiscal impact would depend on whether elevated oil costs are absorbed through excise duty reductions, oil marketing companies or higher retail fuel prices.
Healthy tax collections and potential disinvestment receipts, including from IDBI Bank, could help the government manage fiscal pressures, she added. On the rupee, Sinha said the waiver could improve market sentiment but was unlikely to provide substantial direct support to the currency.
She also stressed that a lasting India-US trade agreement would offer greater economic stability than temporary tariff relief, warning that fresh US tariff threats could emerge. Ramachandran cautioned against immediately entering long-term Russian crude supply agreements without clarity on the waiver's duration.
"The first thing I would say is that it is too early to look at jumping into long-term contracts," he said. He added that refiners would need to assess whether Russian crude discounts and stable supply conditions could be sustained.
GTRI similarly warned India against making permanent trade concessions in exchange for temporary relief. "India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed U.S. pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," Srivastava said. (ANI)

articles.title: India's Tariff Clock Is Now Running And WTO Can't Stop It - Live Law
articles.summary: India's Tariff Clock Is Now Running And WTO Can't Stop It  Live Law
articles.full_text:
U.
S President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O.
Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law on September 18, 2026, after it cleared the House of Representatives 262-159 and the Senate 86-11.
Section 113 of the Act gives the President 30 days from signing a deadline falling around mid-October ,  to fix a tariff of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil or natural gas.
There is a narrow exemption: countries importing less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia, and taking "significant" steps to cut that share further, can escape the duty.
India and China remain the world's two largest buyers of Russian crude.
New Delhi has consistently framed these purchases as a matter of energy security, not as financing for Russia's war in Ukraine.
The Graham Act does not ask why India buys.
It only asks whether India buys, and how much.
That distinction is the real story here, and it is why this moment deserves more than routine trade-news coverage.
This is not simply another round of tariff friction between two trading partners.
It is a legal instrument specifically engineered to operate outside the normal channels of trade law and bilateral diplomacy alike.
The Graham sanctions-tariff regime exposes a structural blind spot in WTO law that has sat unaddressed since 2019: a member facing tariffs framed as "national security" measures has almost no enforceable recourse, because the WTO's own security exception was written to be self-judging, and the one body capable of testing that judgment  the “ Appellate Body ”  has been non-functional for seven years.
India is not losing this argument because its position lacks merit.
It is losing because there is no functioning court left willing, or able, to hear it.

Two distinct U.S. instruments now bear on India, and it is worth separating them clearly. The 2025 "reciprocal tariff" program, layered with an explicit penalty tied to Russian oil purchases, pushed India's effective rate as high as 50% before a partial rollback to 18% under the still-evolving India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA). The Graham Act's Section 113 works differently. It does not penalise anything India sells into the American market. It penalises what India buys from Russia. Under the statute, a country becomes liable the moment it knowingly makes fresh purchases of Russian crude or gas after a statutory cut-off date and ranks among the five largest importers by volume over the preceding twelve months a determination the executive branch is required to review and adjust every 180 days.
This structure runs directly against two foundational WTO obligations. Article I of GATT requires that any tariff advantage or penalty be extended equally to all members , a duty keyed to a country's transactions with a third state sits uneasily with that principle. Article II binds negotiated tariff ceilings, or "bound rates"; a 100% duty imposed outside any formal anti-dumping, countervailing, or safeguard proceeding would, on its face, breach those commitments for most affected goods. Washington's most likely defence is Article XXI, the GATT security exception, which permits a member to take "any action which it considers necessary" to protect its essential security interests, language that makes the accused state the primary judge of its own justification. This is also what separates Section 113 from conventional secondary sanctions. Classic U.S. secondary sanctions, of the sort long used against Iran, operate through Treasury designations against specific banks or companies, entirely outside the tariff schedule. Section 113 instead channels a sanctions-style logic through the ordinary customs tariff itself — a hybrid form that WTO disciplines were never designed to police. 
The timing compounds the legal problem.
Through 2026, India and the United States had methodically de-escalated a difficult relationship: the 25% Russian-oil surcharge was withdrawn, the broader reciprocal tariff cut from 25% to 18%, and both governments built a first-tranche BTA around roughly $500 billion in Indian commitments to purchase American energy, aircraft, and technology.
Section 113 reopens that fight from an entirely different angle.
Because its trigger is Russian-crude volume rather than anything on the BTA's negotiating table, Indian trade negotiators cannot bargain it away through concessions on industrial goods or dairy market access.
It functions as a parallel statutory track, indifferent to the diplomacy specifically built to prevent this kind of confrontation.
India's official response so far reflects this asymmetry.
The Commerce Ministry has told Parliament that it is "working with all stakeholders.
to mitigate the impact," while continuing to defend Russian crude purchases as an energy-security necessity rather than a negotiable trade practice ,  a policy argument, not a legal one, because the legal terrain currently offers little firm ground.
India's WTO membership guarantees it a bound tariff ceiling on paper.
But a statute that treats trade with a third country as its qualifying condition converts what ought to be a rules-based negotiation into a unilateral compliance test, one where New Delhi's leverage is almost entirely political rather than juridical.

The strongest, most defensible criticism of Section 113 is not that it singles out India, but that it contains almost no limiting principle at all. Ordinary U.S. trade remedies , anti-dumping duties, countervailing duties, Section 201 safeguard actions, require a neutral fact-finder, such as a hearing officer or the U.S. International Trade Commission, to first determine that unfair trade practices have actually occurred. Section 113 dispenses with that step entirely: it applies a 100% duty based purely on a third country's dealings with Russia, with no jurisdictional connection to U.S. commerce whatsoever. That is the textbook hallmark of extraterritorial legislation, historically viewed with suspicion by the international community precisely because it lacks a genuine jurisdictional nexus. Compounding this, the qualifying criteria are reviewed by the executive branch itself every 180 days, with no independent adjudicator standing between the trigger and the tariff. Even the Act's own supporters have registered concern: a Senate amendment attempted to stop the President from applying Section 113 to "any country, for any reason," and outside advocacy groups have characterised the bill as ceding additional Article I, Section 8 taxing authority to the executive branch, a domestic constitutional question running alongside the international-law one.
The closest historical parallel is instructive precisely because it never reached a final verdict. When the European Union sought a WTO panel against the extraterritorial Helms-Burton Act in 1996, its formal request filed as WT/DS38/2 ,  argued that the law impeded market access and breached the GATT principle that members should not use trade sanctions to compel other members to alter sovereign policy. The United States, on the record before the Dispute Settlement Body, invoked essential-security justification and warned that pressing the case would pose serious risks to the fledgling WTO. A panel was formally established on November 20, 1996 , but the EU suspended it in April 1997 in exchange for a negotiated understanding with Washington rather than allow a ruling on the merits. The only real WTO test of extraterritorial secondary sanctions ended in diplomatic settlement, not adjudicated precedent a caution India should weigh before assuming litigation offers a cleaner path than talks. The EU's parallel move, a formal "blocking regulation" barring its own companies from complying with the U.S. law, remains a tool New Delhi  has not used it. Closer to home India's own CAATSA stand‑off over India's purchase of S‑400 missiles from Russia was resolved not through any tribunal but through a national‑security waiver granted by Washington in 2022. In every instance the result depended on accommodation not on binding trade law.
If litigation alone cannot rescue India the sensible strategy is layered than singular. India should still file a WTO panel request. India does not expect a ruling because the Appellate Body remains paralyzed but India can build a formal legal record that shows Section 113 triggers a third‑country transactional test rather than a genuine security measure. That record will become a precedent in disputes and a bargaining chip in bilateral talks much as the EU's 1996 filing remained useful even though it never reached a verdict. At the time India should speed up diversification of its crude oil sourcing so that India falls below the Act's "five‑importer" threshold. This is a compliance move under India's energy policy not a concession forced at the negotiating table. While India presses to include Section 113 exposure explicitly in BTA text through a side‑letter or waiver mechanism India seeks an outcome closer to the CAATSA precedent than a courtroom victory. The deeper gap that this episode exposes and the one worth pressing in reform discussions is structural: WTO law currently has no rule that can separate a genuine security tariff from one that is disguised as a security measure to target third‑party conduct. Closing that gap through an interpretation of Article XXI is unfinished business that the Helms‑Burton settlement left unresolved thirty years ago. India, on the receiving end of that same gap has real standing to push the WTO to finally close it.
Author is a 4th year Law student Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University , Lucknow. Views are personal.

The think tank said the waiver could be withdrawn at any time, allowing the US to revive the tariff threat and use it as leverage in bilateral trade negotiations. It urged India to protect its energy security, purchase oil on commercial terms and avoid making permanent trade concessions in return for temporary relief.
Also Read: Trump’s Russian oil tariff waiver buys India time, but not freedom from US pressure
“For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty. India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed US pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions,” GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said.
Trump issued the waiver on October 16 under the newly enacted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (SRIA), which provides for punitive tariffs against Russia and major buyers of its oil. The move came weeks after the legislation became law on September 18.
Why the US may have stepped back
GTRI identified Washington’s own energy requirements, its tariff truce with China and the risk of derailing trade negotiations with India as possible reasons for the waiver.
Under an October 9 agreement with Russia, the US decided to buy Russian diesel to address domestic shortages and high fuel prices. Penalising other countries for purchasing Russian energy while buying it itself could invite accusations of double standards, the think tank said.
Washington has also agreed to hold off on tariff increases against China until January 10 under an arrangement reached during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US last month.
With China shielded from fresh tariff action and the US itself buying Russian diesel, imposing additional duties on India could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations, GTRI said.
“China already had protection against US tariff increases until January 10. The message is clear - US interests determine when penalties apply, while the ability to retaliate helps secure protection. China can push back. India risks repeated pressure unless it demonstrates that coercion carries a cost,” Srivastava said.
Also Read: White House lists investment over $330 billion in US from India
What the waiver means for India
The relief does not remove the underlying tariff threat. According to GTRI, the executive order puts the penalties under the Graham Act on hold by invoking Section 115, which allows the duties to be waived. The waiver has no fixed expiry date, but Washington can withdraw it.
The framework provides for a 500% tariff increase on Russian goods and additional duties of 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian oil making new purchases from October 18, 2026. The US Trade Representative will continue monitoring Russian energy purchases, leaving Washington with the option of reviewing the waiver and restoring the threat, GTRI said.
The think tank also pointed to a shift in India’s oil sourcing. Russia’s share of India’s oil imports fell from 51% in July to 44% in August as purchases shifted towards the US, despite higher prices, and the United Arab Emirates.
GTRI said India should not treat the waiver as a durable change in US policy or make long-term energy decisions around relief that can be reversed. Instead, New Delhi should retain flexibility in its oil purchases and prepare for the possibility of renewed American pressure.

His remarks come amid continuing scrutiny of India's energy trade with Russia following the Ukraine conflict and Western measures targeting Moscow.
India and Russia have maintained energy ties, with New Delhi emphasising the importance of diversifying its energy sources and securing supplies at competitive prices.
The ambassador's remarks underline India's position that energy security and the interests of its 1.4 billion people remain central to its energy policy.

"Third, major that we are working on is negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union, which will help Indian exporters to increase their exports to Russian market and also other markets which are members of the Eurasian Economic Union," Kumar said.

"I think that at the rate at which our trade is growing, we should be able to meet the target that our leaders set in 2024, that is to reach 100 billion dollars of bilateral trade by 2030," he said.

Iran is facing mounting financial pressure after nine months of war, with a US naval blockade costing it $25 billion in lost oil revenue and $350 million in cryptocurrency frozen, according to US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Adm Brad Cooper.
In a video message released on Friday, Cooper said Iran-backed groups across the region, including Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq, were sending money back to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which has funded them for years.
"The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," Cooper said.
He added that the Iranian government was withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including internal security personnel and members of the IRGC.
The financial squeeze comes as the Trump administration maintains a naval blockade and sanctions on Iran, hoping to push Tehran towards a deal that includes concessions on its nuclear programme. However, Iran has yet to respond to a US counterproposal aimed at ending the war.
Cooper said CENTCOM and the US Treasury Department had also frozen $350 million in Iranian cryptocurrency in recent weeks. The naval blockade, meanwhile, had cost Tehran $25 billion in lost oil revenue, he said.
Strait of Hormuz tensions
Cooper attributed the recent increase in Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz to what he described as desperation within the IRGC.
Despite the attacks, the strategic waterway remains open, he said, with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the past week.
The US military has largely paused strikes on Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers around the strait in recent weeks. A US official said the White House ordered the pause to avoid escalating the conflict ahead of the November midterm elections.
US officials are concerned that continued attacks could discourage shipping companies from using the strait, reducing oil supplies and pushing up global prices. They also believe Iran is seeking to raise oil prices and increase pressure on US President Donald Trump ahead of the elections.
Meanwhile, the White House and Qatari mediators are awaiting Tehran's response to Washington's counterproposal to end the war. A US official said the proposal was still under consideration in Tehran.
Regional mediators have urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi not to delay the response until after the midterm elections, warning that there is no guarantee Trump would take a more conciliatory approach afterwards.

At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.
Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.
The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.
Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".
Warning: This article contains distressing details
An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.
Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said.
"I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away."
"There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."
Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".
The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.
Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.
There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.
The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.
Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.
The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away.
The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary".
"We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said.
Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency.
In June, fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahore collapsed.
And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers.

New Delhi [India], October 17 (ANI): Parliamentary and Minority Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju on Saturday firmly declared that India's democratic regime is determined by public mandate through elections, rejecting any attempt to force unconstitutional political upheaval.
In a post on X, he strongly condemned the rhetoric, accusing political rivals and activists of trying to incite chaos and destabilise democratically elected constitutional institutions under the guise of street protests.
Rijiju stated that 'India is not Bangladesh' and asserted that the country's youth are focused on building the nation rather than pulling it down.
' 'Regime Change' !! , ! (Look at those plotting 'regime change'!! Listen loud and clear, India is not Bangladesh!),' Rijiju said.
Underlining that Indian youth are channelising their potential toward nation-building, the Union Minister emphasised their contributions across startups, sports, and technological innovation.
'Indian youth are not fools; they will build India, not destroy India. All genuine Indian youth are winning medals, steering in skilling, innovation, startups, technology & becoming cultural icons!' he wrote.
This comes after Senior Advocate Prashant Bhushan, AISA (All India Students Association) president Neha Bora, and Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera publicly used or discussed the phrase 'regime change' during conferences and press addresses in Delhi in the context of the ongoing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Student activists (including Neha Bora at the Socialist Students Front conference) made references to the Gen-Z student-led political uprising in Bangladesh that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.

BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari also criticised Congress leader P Chidambaram over his remarks defending the use of the phrase "regime change", alleging that taking inspiration from Bangladesh was not democratic and exposing the Opposition's "anarchy".

articles.title: NC and Congress: History of political misadventures - Greater Kashmir

The history of Jammu and Kashmir since 1947 is not merely a story of Pakistani aggression, separatism and terrorism. It is equally a history of political miscalculations, shifting loyalties, personal ambitions and repeated betrayals of democratic principles by the two political parties that dominated its political landscape for decades—the National Conference and Congress. Their relationship, oscillating between political friendship and bitter hostility, created recurring crises of legitimacy and governance. While Pakistan bears direct responsibility for sponsoring cross-border terrorism, the political misadventures of Congress and the National Conference deserve serious scrutiny for creating conditions of alienation and instability that hostile forces subsequently exploited.
The fundamental question is uncomfortable but unavoidable: could the tragic history of terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir have taken a different course had Congress and the National Conference placed democratic institutions above political convenience?
Friendship of Convenience
The political relationship between Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and Jawaharlal Nehru established a pattern that would haunt Jammu and Kashmir for generations. Initially portrayed as an ideological partnership rooted in secularism and democracy, their relationship gradually exposed serious differences concerning political authority, constitutional integration and Kashmir’s future.
Nehru supported Sheikh Abdullah as a central figure in Kashmir’s politics following accession to India. Yet the relationship deteriorated as disagreements emerged over constitutional arrangements and Sheikh Abdullah’s political intentions.
The dismissal and arrest of Sheikh Abdullah in August 1953 represented an extraordinary political reversal. The leader who had enjoyed Nehru’s confidence was suddenly removed from power.
The episode raises serious questions about political judgment on both sides. If Sheikh Abdullah’s political positions were considered dangerous in 1953, why had they previously received such substantial political support? Equally, why did Sheikh Abdullah’s political approach generate such profound uncertainty about Kashmir’s constitutional future?
The consequences extended far beyond two political personalities. The episode became a lasting source of political grievance and distrust.
Democracy Subordinated to Power
The removal of Sheikh Abdullah initiated a prolonged period in which the legitimacy of successive governments became a recurring controversy.
Congress increasingly exercised political influence over Kashmir’s governmental arrangements, while the National Conference’s internal divisions shaped the struggle for authority.
Rather than consolidating democratic confidence, political interventions encouraged the perception that governmental survival depended upon political approval from New Delhi.
The damage was institutional. Political competition increasingly revolved around access to power instead of stable democratic principles.
Such developments provided separatist elements with arguments against the credibility of constitutional politics.
The responsibility for this deterioration cannot be assigned exclusively to one party. Congress and the National Conference both participated in political decisions whose consequences extended beyond their immediate interests.
Principles Sacrificed for Power?
The Indira Gandhi–Sheikh Abdullah Accord of 1975 was another dramatic example of the changing political relationship between Congress and the National Conference.
After more than two decades of confrontation, Sheikh Abdullah returned to power through an arrangement with the Congress leadership.
Political reconciliation is not inherently objectionable. Indeed, accommodation can strengthen democratic stability. However, the accord exposed the striking transformation of political positions that had previously appeared irreconcilable.
The same political establishment that had supported Sheikh Abdullah’s removal facilitated his return. What had changed so fundamentally that yesterday’s political adversary became today’s indispensable partner?
The accord restored Sheikh Abdullah to office but did not permanently resolve the underlying tensions concerning constitutional identity, regional aspirations and political trust.
Instead of creating enduring institutional reconciliation, Kashmir’s political stability remained excessively dependent upon understandings between powerful individuals.
Another Assault on Democratic Credibility
The dismissal of Farooq Abdullah’s government in 1984 represented another damaging chapter.
Following Sheikh Abdullah’s death, Farooq Abdullah emerged as the principal leader of the National Conference. His relationship with Congress deteriorated, eventually culminating in a political rebellion led by G. M. Shah.
The formation of a rival government with Congress support was widely criticised as an exercise in political manipulation.
The episode reinforced the perception that elected governments could be destabilised through political manoeuvring.
For a sensitive border region already experiencing political uncertainty, the consequences were particularly serious.
Congress pursued immediate political advantage, while the National Conference’s internal divisions exposed weaknesses within its own political organisation.
The larger casualty was public confidence in democratic stability.
A Historic Failure
The 1987 Jammu and Kashmir Assembly elections constitute perhaps the most consequential political episode in the history of Congress–National Conference cooperation.
The two parties contested the elections in alliance against opposition forces, including the Muslim United Front.
Widespread allegations of electoral manipulation, intimidation and irregularities seriously damaged the credibility of the electoral process.
Several political observers and historical studies have identified the disputed elections as an important factor contributing to the alienation of sections of Kashmiri youth and the subsequent growth of militancy.
The precise relationship between individual electoral grievances and decisions to join armed organisations requires careful historical examination. Nevertheless, the broader political consequences were profound.
A democratic system that fails to convince citizens of the fairness of electoral competition risks losing its most important source of legitimacy.
The National Conference and Congress must face political accountability for their conduct during this critical period.
The tragedy was that Pakistan-backed terrorist organisations subsequently exploited the disillusionment arising from domestic political failures.
The 1987 elections remain a powerful reminder that manipulating democratic institutions for short-term political gain can produce consequences far beyond the immediate electoral contest.
Political Leadership’s Failure
Pakistan’s responsibility for sponsoring, training, financing and supporting terrorist organisations operating in Jammu and Kashmir is central to any honest account of the insurgency.
The emergence of militancy also reflected regional developments, radicalisation, cross-border networks and the consequences of the Afghan conflict.
However, external aggression becomes more dangerous when domestic political institutions are weakened.
The recurring conflicts between Congress and the National Conference contributed to an environment in which constitutional politics was frequently viewed with suspicion.
Their repeated political confrontations, followed by opportunistic accommodations, weakened confidence in the consistency of governance.
Pakistan exploited these vulnerabilities to promote separatism and armed violence.
It would be historically inaccurate to claim that Congress and the National Conference alone caused terrorism. Yet it would be equally irresponsible to ignore the role of their political decisions in weakening democratic legitimacy during crucial periods.
Pakistan must answer for the terrorism it sponsored; Congress and the National Conference must answer for the political failures that helped create opportunities for its exploitation.
The Human Cost 
The consequences of terrorism devastated Jammu and Kashmir.
Thousands lost their lives. Security personnel, civilians, political workers and public officials became victims of violence. Kashmiri Pandits suffered targeted killings, intimidation and mass displacement. Ordinary Muslim families also endured terrorism, coercion and prolonged insecurity.
Economic development suffered, tourism declined, educational opportunities were disrupted and generations grew up amid violence.
The political leadership cannot escape historical scrutiny by treating this tragedy merely as an unfortunate consequence of external aggression.
The central issue is whether earlier political decisions could have strengthened democratic institutions sufficiently to reduce the vulnerabilities exploited by militant organisations.
For Congress and the National Conference, that question remains unanswered.
The Politics of Contradiction
Another striking feature of National Conference politics has been its alternating emphasis on autonomy and cooperation with national political establishments.
The party has repeatedly presented itself as the guardian of Kashmir’s regional identity while entering alliances with Congress at different historical stages.
Congress has similarly adopted changing positions concerning Kashmir’s constitutional and political arrangements.
Constitutional demands and political alliances are legitimate democratic activities. The criticism arises when contradictory political narratives are used to secure electoral advantage without offering clarity about long-term governance.
Such inconsistency encouraged political uncertainty and allowed competing forces to exploit public confusion.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised the India GDP growth forecast to 7% for FY27 and FY28, citing resilient domestic demand, services activity, and favourable demographic trends. The revised outlook places India’s projected growth above the global economy’s expected expansion of 3.1% in 2026. For Indian entrepreneurs and business owners, the estimates offer a view of expected economic activity, while inflation and energy costs remain important factors.
India’s growth outlook strengthens against global trends
In its October 2026 World Economic Outlook, the IMF raised its growth estimate for India in FY27 to 7%, up from 6.4% projected in July. It also revised its FY28 forecast upwards to 7% from 6.7%.
The IMF identified an expanding domestic market, favourable demographic trends, and continued structural reforms as factors supporting India’s growth potential. Domestic consumption and services activity have also helped the economy maintain momentum despite uncertainty in international markets.
The Fund expects the global economy to grow by 3.1% in 2026, slightly above its July estimate of 3%. Global growth stood at 3.5% in 2025. For 2027, the IMF projects growth of 3.4%, unchanged from its previous forecast.
India’s projected growth rate is more than twice the expected global rate for 2026. The figures reflect different growth paths across economies, with domestic demand and services supporting India’s outlook.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has projected growth of 7.1% for FY27, slightly above the IMF’s India GDP growth forecast of 7%.
For businesses, the India GDP growth forecast provides context for planning around consumer demand, operating capacity, and investment. However, actual results will depend on conditions across individual industries and changes in domestic and international markets.
Oil prices and inflation remain key economic risks
Higher crude oil prices remain a potential source of pressure for India, which relies heavily on imports to meet its energy needs.
The IMF’s October outlook assumes an average crude oil price of $95.74 per barrel in 2026, an increase of around 41% from 2025. It expects the average to fall to $87.39 per barrel in 2027.
Sustained high oil prices could raise India’s import bill and put pressure on its current account balance. Higher energy costs can also increase transport, manufacturing, and other operating expenses for businesses. If companies pass these costs on to consumers, household purchasing power may come under pressure.
The IMF expects India’s consumer inflation to reach 5% in FY27 before easing to 4.4% in FY28. It also projects the current account deficit to reach 1.5% of gross domestic product in FY27.
Globally, inflation is expected to reach 4.7% in 2026 before moderating to 4.1% in 2027. Higher energy and food prices are among the factors behind the projection.
The IMF also noted that investment linked to artificial intelligence has supported economic activity in some parts of the world, although the benefits have varied across economies. Energy price increases and uncertainty in international markets remain risks to the global outlook.
India’s revised forecast points to continued economic expansion over the next 2 fiscal years. The pace of growth will also depend on domestic spending, inflation, energy prices, and global trade and investment conditions.

articles.summary: From stability to growth  The Sunday Times, Sri Lanka
articles.full_text:
View(s):
In our Kussi Amma Sera column on September 20, we alluded to this possibility after comments by Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa and CCC Chairman Krishan Balendra who went on record saying there is a need to go for another programme after the current IMF arrangement ends in March 2027. “These (IMF) conversations – though the government exudes confidence in meeting the 2028 and onwards foreign repayment schedule (one way is to substantially increase export earnings and reach $5 billion in IT services’ exports) – need to start taking place now, without any delay,” I wrote in that column.
At the CCC event, during a fireside chat, the President was quoted as saying, “Discussions are ongoing about a potential agreement that would prioritise economic growth while maintaining the progress achieved under the existing IMF-backed programme. The current IMF programme was about stabilising the economy. The next discussion should be on how to maintain this stability and increase our growth.”
The key to these conversations is the need to move, rather swiftly, to a growth-based economy from the stability-centric one. Caught under the twin effects of the COVID-19 crisis and the subsequent economic crisis, largely due to acute mismanagement of the economy, Sri Lanka hurriedly sought an IMF bailout package. Without that, the country – lacking in much-needed dollars and tax revenue – would have been doomed. The IMF saved the day and thankfully the present NPP government, taking over the reins after its electoral win in November 2024, decided to continue with the programme. The fund programme has brought the much-needed stability to the economy, cut wasteful public spending, regained confidence and resulted in an increase in worker remittances, export earnings and tourism receipts.
Thus the economic focus has shifted to moving from stability to growth and this is where today’s conversation is taking place. As I opened the office room window to allow the wind to flow in, the home phone rang. Calling on this Thursday morning was Arthika, my nonsensical economist friend also known as good-for-nothing Somey.
“I say…….so the government is now considering another IMF programme,” he said. “It looks like that going by various statements in the public space,” I said.
“I too thought this was necessary otherwise, we would have gone back to dismantling the fundamentals of the IMF way-forward and the discipline in public spending management, a key pillar of the IMF programme,” he said. “Perhaps the President, when he presents the budget for 2027, will detail the steps to be taken on the need for another programme and the way forward,” I said. “The President is also bound to explain the need to move forward with a growth-centric economy from one that is focused currently on stability and recovery – from the economic crisis,” he added.
The Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) in its State of the Economy 2026 report released this week said durable growth must sustain macroeconomic stability while raising productivity, complemented by higher private investment, a more competitive and diversified export sector and more effective use of scarce public resources. The challenge then is to accelerate growth without reopening the fiscal and external vulnerabilities that contributed to the crisis, it said.
The report said Sri Lanka has made significant progress since the economic crisis of 2022. Economic growth has continued into 2026, with real GDP expanding by 5 per cent in both 2024 and 2025 and 4.7 per cent in the first half of 2026. Inflation has moderated substantially from its 2022 peak, external debt restructuring has advanced, and foreign reserves have been rebuilt to more comfortable levels.
“However, the country now faces a more complex challenge in ensuring that recovery evolves into a durable growth process that can withstand future shocks and deliver broad-based improvements in living standards,” the report said.
Through a series of practical policy recommendations across trade, fiscal management, labour markets, urbanisation, energy, agriculture, social protection and human capital development, the report set out a roadmap for transforming recovery into a more resilient, inclusive and productive growth trajectory.
It added that Sri Lanka can achieve its long-term development ambitions, but only by pursuing reforms that build competitiveness, strengthen resilience and ensure that the benefits of growth are broadly shared.
Welcoming the ‘impressive’ improvement in macroeconomic indicators, the IMF in a report last week said the Sri Lankan economy has proved remarkably resilient to successive shocks. But it pointed out: “It is not just how Sri Lanka can maintain short-term stability, but how it can protect that stability and convert it into durable, sustainable and inclusive growth. It links three core pillars — macroeconomic resilience, clean governance and productivity-enhancing structural reforms.”
Taking a break, I walked to the kitchen and to my delight there were piping hot ‘maalu paans’ on the table. I heard Aldoris, the choon-paan karaya, coming to the gate in his music-blaring tuk-tuk, happily playing a song now that a controversial tax on music has been suspended.
Grabbing a ‘maalu paan’ and a mug of tea, I was walking back to my room when I heard the conversation by the trio under the margosa tree. “Mae davas wala eka, eka deshapalagnayan saha egollange golayanwa ath-adanguwata gannawa (All kinds of politicians and their henchmen are being arrested these days),” said Kussi Amma Sera. “Pramanawath saakshi athi kiyala mama balaporoththu wenava nathnam kattiya hithanna puluwan deshapalana paliganeem kiyala (I hope they have enough evidence against these persons otherwise it would be seen as a political vendetta),” noted Serapina. “Eth aanduwa kiyanawaney mae okkoma nadu daala thiyenney yahapalana aanduwa kaly kiyala 2015-2019 athara. Eh hinda saakshi athi-ney (But the government says these are all cases filed during the Yahapalanaya regime in 2015-2019, so there is bound to be some evidence),” added Mabel Rasthiyadu.
With the focus on growth, it would be interesting to see what unfolds in the budget. The President and his ministers have gone on record saying that taxes would be reduced thereby reducing the burden on the people. However, increased taxes are essential for public spending particularly on proposed new highways, an increased education budget, health and welfare. Over to you, Mr. President! What do you have in store for us to alleviate our present ills?
