articles.title: Need to move beyond the plateau in India-US relations - The Sunday Guardian
articles.summary: Need to move beyond the plateau in India-US relations  The Sunday Guardian
articles.full_text:
Notwithstanding the expansion and strengthening of ties across various spheres, some wrinkles began to appear in India-US relations at the very start of President Donald Trump’s second term.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was among the early visitors to the White House in Trump 2.0, visiting on February 12-13, 2025. Despite accusations by the US that India was the “tariff king”, a difficult country to do business with, and that it was fleecing the US market, being on the wrong side of history and funding Russia’s invasion of Ukraine—remarks expressed in an undiplomatic manner by key members of the Trump administration—India remained reluctant to publicly acknowledge strains in the relationship. This was despite being penalised with an additional 25% tariff for importing Russian oil and facing accusations from opposition parties that the Modi government lacked the courage to stand up to a bullying US.
The controversy surrounding the US role, if any, in mediating the ceasefire between India and Pakistan following Operation Sindoor created further unease. The warmth and bonhomie extended to Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff, General Munir, in the aftermath of the bloody terrorist attack in Pahalgam exacerbated the situation.
The current US Ambassador, Sergio Gor, a close confidant of President Trump, has been making vigorous efforts to improve relations between the two countries. He has met Indian ministers, chief ministers and industry leaders, promoting bilateral business and investment. He has also sought to smooth ruffled feathers by repeatedly emphasising, in glowing terms, the warmth and personal friendship between the Indian Prime Minister and the US President. He is rightly credited with facilitating the signing of the Interim Framework Agreement in February 2026, which resulted in the lifting of the 25% punitive duty imposed on imports of Russian oil. He also facilitated India’s entry into Pax Silica.
However, the long-drawnout and rigorously negotiated trade deal remains inconclusive. Understandably, the reluctance to acknowledge problems publicly has now faded, and neither side is shy about admitting that everything is not hunkydory. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting, hosted by the Munich Security Conference (MSC) in Delhi on October 4-5, 2026, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman plainly stated that IndiaUS trade negotiations had reached a “plateau”. She also made it clear that it would be very difficult for either side to make further concessions or compromises. In its pursuit of a narrower trade deficit, the US has weaponised tariffs and is seeking an agreement outside the established norms of global trade.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar was even more outspoken in his remarks at the meeting. Reminding the audience that India is a strategic partner of the US, not an ally, he stressed that, like the US, India pursues an “India First” policy and exercises its “strategic autonomy” when differences arise. He drove home the point that, by pursuing unilateral policies without regard for their negative repercussions on others, the US has, by its own choice, become a lonelier power in the world. Current US policies have prompted various countries to recalibrate their engagement with Washington.
Jaishankar also minced no words in pointing out the US’s insensitivity towards India in its dealings with Pakistan, which has used terrorism as a state policy against India. He shared his thoughts on how the idea of a G2 impacts countries such as India. While acknowledging that India and the US enjoy substantial cooperation in trade, technology, defence, nuclear energy and space, he stressed that Russia has been a trusted partner for decades. India, therefore, does not subscribe to the Cold War-era “loyalty test”. In the prevailing global scenario, India follows a path of multi-alignment, under which countries can form groups or partnerships, or enter into agreements with whichever countries their national interests warrant.
The increase in H-1B visa fees, the suspension of TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant from the PERM (Permanent Labour Certification Programme), and Capgemini’s exclusion have further soured relations. With little time for the Quad and an unmistakable eagerness to sustain the thaw with China, India feels that its standing as a strategic partner has diminished in Washington’s reckoning. US Vice-President JD Vance’s likening of H-1B visa holders and Indian tech workers to indentured servants was particularly unfortunate. Are the heads of Microsoft and Meta, NASA scientists, business school deans and the 45 doctors of AAPI indentured labourers?
The message in Prime Minister Modi’s remarks at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum could not have been lost on Washington: “Things that once connected the world are now being turned into weapons. Supply chains, energy, minerals, payment systems, and technology are increasingly becoming instruments of pressure and dominance.”
India cannot wield critical minerals and technologies as leverage in the way China can. But, having purchased US$25 billion worth of defence equipment and energy supplies worth over US$14 billion, with orders for dozens of Boeing civilian aircraft also in the pipeline, should India not use these commitments as leverage in future negotiations?
With an economy that the IMF projects will grow at 7%, a population of 1.4 billion, including an aspirational young demographic, 200,000 startups and 2,000 GCCs, India stands out as a stable and trusted partner in today’s turbulent, disrupted and unpredictable world. India is not a strategic rival of the US, and more Americans view India favourably than China. While the pro-MAGA approach has gained ground under Trump 2.0, the advantages of closer ties with India must be consistently highlighted at Republican Party fundraisers, particularly among the Indian diaspora and pro-India members of academia.
India is not seeking a rupture in relations, but neither should it be too meek to speak out when it matters most. I believe that this is what India has been doing of late, as reflected in the recent speeches of the Prime Minister, Finance Minister and External Affairs Minister.
At the same time, diversifying relations more purposefully with the EU, ASEAN, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Africa and Latin America will help hedge against any losses in the US market.
Surendra Kumar is a former ambassador of India.

articles.title: WE SEEK NEW PARTNERS LIKE INDIA AS U.S. TRADE BARRIERS RISE: CZECHIA DY PM - The Sunday Guardian
articles.summary: WE SEEK NEW PARTNERS LIKE INDIA AS U.S. TRADE BARRIERS RISE: CZECHIA DY PM  The Sunday Guardian
articles.full_text:
In an exclusive conversation with NewsX Foreign Affairs Editor Sukanya Saha, Havlícek discusses why India matters to Europe’s economic future, whether New Delhi can help bring Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, and how Europe should respond to Washington’s shifting trade and energy policies. He also shares his views on Ukraine’s NATO ambitions and the prospect of closer ties between Canada and the European Union.
Q. Bilateral trade has crossed $4 billion, but how do we take it to the next level? What, according to you, is the biggest outcome of this visit, so far?
A. Bilateral trade of $4 billion is a good level, but we can and must do more. The India-EU Free Trade Agreement, which is expected to be signed in the coming weeks or months, will create a market of 2 billion people. That’s an enormous opportunity. Czechia is an export-oriented, engineering-driven and highly industrialised economy, so there is huge potential for collaboration. I’m here not just to offer our products, but also to explore joint projects and investment opportunities in India. We know India’s economic strategy is built around Make in India. Our ambition is to build long-term ties through investment and joint ventures with Indian businesses. That’s why I’ve brought a business delegation with me.”
Q. When will the India-EU FTA become a reality? Negotiations have concluded, but businesses are waiting. When do you expect the agreement to enter into force, and what is holding up implementation?
A. The agreement is currently going through the ratification process. I hope it will be formally signed in November or December this year. That would send an extremely important signal to businesses and encourage greater collaboration with India. I’ve been working with India for 20 years, having come from the business sector, and I’ve seen the country’s remarkable growth over the past 10 to 15 years. India is not only the world’s most populous country but also a major force in research and development and new technologies. There’s tremendous potential here.
Q. Do you think Czechia risks being overshadowed by larger European economies in capitalising on the India-EU FTA? If not, then which Czech industries stand to benefit most from better access to the Indian market?
A. From India’s perspective, Czechia may be a small country, but we are a major industrial and engineering hub in Europe. We have strong capabilities in aircraft manufacturing, and we are among the few countries globally that can produce complete aircraft. I met India’s Civil Aviation Minister Kinjarapu Ram Mohan Naidu, and we discussed opportunities to develop and manufacture aircraft jointly with Indian companies. We also have a strong automotive and transport industry, producing cars, buses, trains and trams. Companies such as Volkswagen, Hyundai, Toyota, Mercedes, Iveco and Tata have a presence in Czechia, while Škoda Transportation is a major producer of trains. There is considerable scope for collaboration, including supplying components and trains to India. With Tata and Škoda expanding their presence, the opportunities are significant.
Q. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member. What would that actually mean, and could this model reshape Europe’s partnerships beyond its borders?
A. It may have come as a surprise, but the European Union is open to working with all important countries. Economies such as Germany, Czechia and France are highly industrialised and export-oriented, so why not collaborate more closely with Canada? The key question is what form this arrangement would take. If it means lower tariffs or tariff-free trade, that would be a positive step. Closer trade ties would benefit European producers and Canadian businesses alike.
Q. But it was after Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canada that von der Leyen floated the idea of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member. Could such an arrangement risk creating new trade frictions with the US, particularly over tariffs?
A. The US remains an extremely important partner for Europe, with trade between them roughly ten times greater than between Europe and Canada. We must strengthen transatlantic ties, but when the US puts up trade barriers, Europe has to look for new partnerships. That means working more closely with Canada, Latin America, India and other Asian countries. Europe has great people, universities and a rich history, but we are losing competitiveness, particularly because our energy costs are much higher than in the US. That’s the reality. If Europe wants to remain competitive, we must look beyond our borders and deepen cooperation with countries like India.
Q. Shifting focus to the Russia Ukraine conflict now, what would it take to achieve lasting peace between Moscow and Kyiv, and what role, if any, do you see for India in that process?
A. The war between Russia and Ukraine is a major tragedy, and it has been going on for more than four years. Russia is the aggressor, and we stand with Ukraine. At the same time, the sooner the war ends, the fewer compromises may be needed in the end. Any peace agreement must respect Ukraine’s interests. I believe India could play a very important role in this process, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of the most respected leaders in the world. India is a global power, and I can see it playing a constructive role in bringing the parties closer to peace. India also inspires me, and there is enormous scope to strengthen our cooperation through trade and investment. PM Modi is one of the most respected and popular leaders in the world. I had the opportunity to meet him previously alongside my Prime Minister, and it was a remarkable experience. I am a great admirer of Prime Minister Modi, and it would be an honour to meet him again
The US is trying to push for a resolution, but Russia has yet to respond. I will be travelling to Ukraine with a business delegation for a month, where we plan to meet politicians, ministers, possibly President Zelenskyy, as well as Ukrainian entrepreneurs. This is a deeply sensitive issue for Czechia. Ukraine is our neighbour, and we share historical and linguistic ties. Around 500,000 Ukrainian refugees live in Czechia, and many are contributing to our economy, working across manufacturing and services. I hope Prime Minister Modi can play an important role as a mediator in bringing the sides closer to peace.
Q. Is Ukraine’s eventual NATO membership still on the table, and could it become part of a future peace settlement?
A. It’s not possible while the war is ongoing. It is a question that would have to be considered in the future.
Q. Speaking of the Iran crisis, there’s a joke that the landlocked Czech Republic is sending its “entire navy” to the Gulf. Jokes aside, why did Prague decide to stand with Washington on Hormuz, and what is the strategic objective?
A. Europe is facing a serious energy price problem. It is not necessarily a question of supply, but of cost. Gas prices in Europe are many times higher than in the US, pushing up electricity costs and hurting our competitiveness. European companies are moving production to the US, China and Asia, and we have to stop that. The war in Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East, and the EU’s Green Deal all contribute to the pressure on energy prices. Europe needs to rethink its approach to reflect the changing global situation.
Q. Trump threatened India and China with 100% tariffs for buying Russian oil, but is now buying diesel from Moscow himself and rebuking Ukraine for striking Russian energy infrastructure. Meanwhile, India is pushing for a ceasefire initiative in the Black Sea region. Does this double standard undermine peace efforts and prolong the conflict in Ukraine? Also, whose side is Washington really on right now?
A. Czechia believes in maintaining strong partnerships with both the US and the European Union. President Trump is pragmatic and has tried to end the war in Ukraine, but Russia has yet to respond. Decisions like these must be discussed with European partners in advance. Europe is not an enemy of the US. It may be a competitor, but it is also a partner, and American decisions have a direct impact on us. Energy prices are already much higher in Europe than in the US, and we need to communicate these concerns to President Trump and his administration. I cannot predict what will happen next. Trump often makes announcements as part of a broader negotiating strategy, and the position may change within days. We must also remember that the EU has 27 member states and governments, so reaching a common position takes time. The US can make decisions much faster, and that difference must be understood.
Q. Beyond the meetings and negotiations, what experience or encounter during your visit has stayed with you the most?
A. I really love India. I come from a business background and have had the opportunity to export products to India, working with trading partners in Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Mumbai, Udaipur and Jaipur. It is an amazing and unique country, shaped by its philosophies, values, and strong trading traditions. India also has a remarkable global presence. Your people speak excellent English, Indian professionals are highly successful in the US and Europe, and your managers are making their mark in major international corporations. Your universities and talent have also built a strong reputation internationally. India is a country that inspires me. I see enormous potential for collaboration at the highest level, and I will do everything I can to strengthen our ties and promote mutual trade and investment.

articles.title: The Indian growth story: Why the post-pandemic boom is different - The Times of India
articles.summary: The Indian growth story: Why the post-pandemic boom is different  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
India may have slipped to the sixth spot in the list of the world’s largest economies, but its GDP growth continues to defy estimates by both domestic and global institutions. At 7% plus, India is the world’s fastest growing major economy and what stands out in the current phase is the resilience amid multiple, persistent, and emerging global uncertainties.
Kyunghoon Kim, Head of India & South Asia Team at Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) has said that India’s growth has set to surpass 7% for the fifth consecutive year.
“India’s economy rebounded by 9.7% in 2021, then grew by more than 7% in each of the next four years. That makes five consecutive years of growth above 7%, matching the 2003–2007 run, when India attracted global attention as one of the BRIC economies,” he says in a thread on X (formerly Twitter).
In the post, Kim noted that India’s average annual economic growth between 2021 and 2025 was 7.83%. This was the second-highest five-year average in data going back to 1960, just behind the 7.89% recorded between 2003 and 2007.
India’s economy contracted by 5.8% in 2020 during the pandemic before rebounding with growth of 9.7% in 2021. It then expanded by more than 7% in each of the following four years, according to Kim.
Kim said that if current forecasts hold, India could surpass that record.
He also pointed to how economists, including himself, have repeatedly revised their growth projections upwards as quarterly GDP figures came in stronger than expected.
The point of his comparison was not simply the sharp rebound after the pandemic, but the economy’s ability to sustain rapid growth over several subsequent years.
Several things stand out in this growth: for one, the economy is now operating on a completely different scale.
As Kim notes, India’s GDP was just over $1 trillion in 2007; now it is nearly $4 trillion. “The same 7% growth rate therefore represents a much larger expansion,” he says.
The post pandemic era
In 2020, when the Covid pandemic dealt a major blow to the global economy, India too took a major hit to its economy and GDP contracted sharply. Since then, the economy’s bounceback has been stronger than expected, consistently beating estimates by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
At the end of FY2021, the size of the Indian economy by nominal GDP was $2.6 trillion. At the end of FY2027, it is projected to be $4.15 trillion - that’s an almost 60% rise in just six years despite the pandemic, Russia-Ukraine war, Trump’s trade policies and 50% tariffs, and now the ongoing US-Iran war.
Five consecutive years of growth above 7%
What’s also noteworthy is that India depends on the world for 90% of its crude oil needs and the US-Iran conflict choked a crucial oil supply passage for the country - the Strait of Hormuz. Economists around the world warned that the Indian economy would see a notable hit from the war. Yet, the first quarter estimates of 7.8% have beaten all estimates. Inflation has risen, but it is still within RBI’s target range.
So what’s working for India?
It’s the size of its domestic market and a demographic dividend that is paying off along with key reforms by the government and a proactive monetary policy management by the RBI. The country has been pushing for self-sufficiency and schemes like the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme have made it into a key export hub, especially for electronics.
Kim acknowledged that India continues to face challenges, while arguing that its economic performance deserves attention given the country’s population of around 1.4 billion.
GDP Growth Forecasts See Sharp Upward Revisions
Kim also highlighted recent upward revisions to India’s growth outlook by major institutions. According to him the upgrades are particularly notable when viewed against India’s growth record since the pandemic.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its growth projection for India in the current year from 6.4% to 7%. The revision follows similar upgrades by several other institutions, including the World Bank, Asian Development Bank (ADB), S&P and Moody's.
These changes came after official figures put India's GDP growth in the first quarter at 7.8%. Most international agencies now expect the economy to expand by 6.9% to 7% in the current fiscal year.
India's GDP Growth Forecasts See Upward Revisions
IMF has endorsed India's revised approach to calculating gross domestic product, saying the new methodology conforms to sound statistical practices and recommendations made by the international financial institution.
Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, called the change a "welcome development". He said India's updated method of measuring GDP was consistent with the guidance issued by the IMF's statistics department.
In its latest World Economic Outlook, the IMF said that the global economy has remained resilient despite several shocks in recent years, projecting worldwide growth of 3.4% in 2026.
India remains among the fastest-growing major economies, with growth in 2026 projected at 7%. This reflects stronger-than-expected momentum, supported by resilient domestic demand and robust services activity," the IMF said.
India and Germany have recorded the largest upward revisions to their growth forecasts. In contrast, Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to contract by 3.3% this year, following a five-percentage-point reduction in its growth outlook.
Explaining India's improved prospects, the IMF said: "India stands out with upward revisions, reflecting sustained momentum and growing evidence of stronger growth potential supported by favorable demographic dynamics, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms.”
The report also drew attention to India's efforts to broaden its trade relationships. It cited the country's trade agreements with the UK and the European Union, which are expected to reduce tariffs and ease restrictions on services trade. These arrangements could also "facilitate adjustments to recent trade policy changes".
US tariff measures have prompted countries around the world to pursue a series of trade agreements. India, too, has advanced free trade agreements (FTAs) that had remained under negotiation for years.
The Indian economy continues to surprise on the upside, and despite the sharp rupee depreciation which led to its nominal GDP not rising as much in dollar terms, the economy continues to hold strong. As per latest IMF projections, India is expected to become the third largest economy after the US and China by 2031.

Washington: The US has scrapped a policy to grant automatic extensions to work permits, including those of spouses of H-1 B visa holders, a move that could affect several foreign professionals, including Indians, while their applications for extension of employment authorisation documents (EADs) remain pending.
Experience a more refined e-paper today
An interim rule to this effect was issued on October 30 last year and the US Citizenship and Immigration Services codified the final rule on Wednesday.
The 540-day automatic extension for EAD permits was introduced during President Joe Biden's tenure in May 2022 to reduce the number of renewal applicants to avoid processing delays by USCIS. The rule was re-issued as a temporary measure in April 2024 and granted an indefinite extension in December 2024.
The interim rule issued last October removed the automatic extension of EADs for categories including adjustment of status applicants, H-4 spouses, asylum applicants, refugees and asylees, and temporary protected status (TPS) beneficiaries.
Students on F-1 applying for a STEM extension of employment authorisation are not affected by the elimination of the maximum 540-day auto-extension. This category continues to receive a 180-day auto-extension upon timely filing of their STEM EAD application.
Spouses of persons on L and E category visas remain work-authorised “incident to status” and do not require an EAD.
The Trump administration also proposed a new rule eliminating a longstanding practice of giving deference to prior approvals when adjudicating extension petitions for certain nonimmigrant workers.
The move could significantly increase scrutiny of previously routine visa extensions – including H-1B visas – and lead to longer wait times.
If the proposed rule is implemented, USCIS officers would be instructed to independently evaluate each extension petition on its own merits rather than giving deference to prior determinations.
Enhanced scrutiny may lead to more Requests for Evidence (RFEs), extensive documentation requirements, longer adjudication timelines, and increased legal and administrative costs associated with extension filings.
Employers may need to approach extension petitions much like initial filings, ensuring that eligibility is fully documented regardless of prior approvals.
The Department of Homeland Security has invited comments on the proposal till November 13.
"I strongly condemn the Trump administration decision to codify and finalise the elimination of the 540-day automatic work permit extension," said Ajay Jain Bhutoria, former White House advisor and immigration attorney.
"This regressive policy shift is a devastating blow to hardworking legal immigrants, H-4 spouses, healthcare workers, and families who rely on employment authorisation documents to build their lives and contribute to America's prosperity,” Bhutoria added.

Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel could strengthen India’s case for continuing discounted crude purchases from Russia.
US President Donald Trump’s decision to relax sanctions on Russian diesel exports could give India greater bargaining power in its energy trade negotiations with Washington. The move comes as New Delhi faces continued pressure over its purchases of discounted Russian crude oil.
Analysts believe the decision could help India challenge the consistency of US sanctions policy, seek exemptions from punitive trade measures and strengthen its position as an independent diplomatic player in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
The policy shift comes amid elevated global energy prices and supply disruptions linked to the US-Iran conflict. Brent crude was trading around $105 per barrel on October 13.
Under the arrangement announced by Trump, Russia is expected to supply additional diesel to the US and international markets in phases.
The proposed supply schedule includes:
More than 300,000 tonnes immediately
Another 500,000 tonnes in November
An additional 1 million tonnes shortly thereafter
A further 3 million tonnes within a relatively short period, depending on Russian refinery conditions
The US Treasury has also issued a temporary licence easing sanctions restrictions on Russian diesel shipments.
The decision represents a significant shift in Washington’s approach towards Russian energy supplies, particularly as the US continues to discourage other countries from purchasing Russian oil.
Ukrainian and European Union officials have criticised the arrangement, warning that increased Russian fuel exports could generate additional revenue for Moscow's military operations.
India has faced sustained pressure from Washington over its imports of discounted Russian crude since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed into law by Trump, provides for tariffs of up to 100% on imports from major purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas, subject to specified exceptions.
India is among the countries potentially exposed to these measures.
However, Washington's willingness to ease restrictions on Russian diesel to address its own energy requirements could strengthen India's argument that national energy security should be treated consistently.
India can press for exemptions while continuing to diversify its crude oil suppliers and expand opportunities in refined petroleum exports.
The broader argument is that energy security considerations influencing American policy should also be recognised when evaluating India's purchases of Russian crude.
India has emerged as a supplier of refined petroleum products to Russia, where Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries have contributed to domestic fuel shortages.
This changing trade relationship underlines the complexity of global energy markets, where crude oil imports and refined fuel exports are increasingly influenced by supply disruptions and sanctions.
The immediate benefit for India may be diplomatic rather than commercial. Although Washington has relaxed restrictions on specific Russian diesel shipments, its broader sanctions framework targeting major buyers of Russian oil remains in place.
Consequently, Indian exporters could still face the threat of substantial US tariffs.
The diesel arrangement has weakened Washington's political justification for penalising India over Russian energy purchases. However, New Delhi would benefit more from using the development to negotiate practical concessions than from directly challenging Washington over inconsistencies in its policies.
India could prioritise obtaining sanctions exemptions, securing greater clarity over future trade restrictions and preserving flexibility in its energy sourcing.
Such an approach would allow New Delhi to protect its economic interests without unnecessarily complicating its broader strategic relationship with the US.
The developments come as global crude oil markets remain under pressure from geopolitical tensions in West Asia.
Brent crude was trading around $105 per barrel on October 13, following a sharp increase linked to attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi militants.
Higher energy prices are a particular concern for India, which depends heavily on imported crude oil.
A sustained increase in oil prices could raise India's import bill, put pressure on the rupee and contribute to domestic inflation.
Access to competitively priced Russian crude therefore remains commercially important, even as Indian refiners seek alternative suppliers.
Srinivaasan Balakrishnan of the Indic Researchers Forum believes Washington's decision demonstrates how domestic economic priorities can influence sanctions policy.
For India, the larger challenge is to translate strategic autonomy into stronger economic resilience through diversified energy supplies and reduced exposure to geopolitical disruptions.
Trump's Russian diesel arrangement does not automatically remove the tariff and sanctions risks facing India.
However, it could strengthen New Delhi's negotiating position in three important areas:
Energy trade: Seek exemptions and more consistent treatment for Russian crude purchases.
US relations: Push for greater predictability in trade and sanctions policies.
Global diplomacy: Expand India's role in negotiations aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Iranian accounting student facing death sentence over social media post  The Times of India"मेरी आवाज़ ही, पहचान है": Condemned to hang in Mashhad over an online post, 23-year-old student Najmeh Amini begs the world to be her voice from death row, clinging to hope for h...

An Iranian court sentenced 23-year-old Najmeh Amini to death for blasphemy over a social media post. Amid outcry by rights groups, Amini has released an audio message from prison.
A 23-year-old Iranian woman has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social media post, according to rights monitors, after she was arrested during nationwide anti-government protests earlier this year.
Najmeh Amini, an accounting student from Mashhad, said in an audio message from prison that the judiciary issued her death sentence on September 16, 2026. The sentence is not final and can be appealed before Iran’s Supreme Court.
Amini was arrested by security forces on January 31 during protests against Iran’s fundamentalist regime, which were met with a deadly crackdown. At least 7,000 were reported killed, while more than 50,000 people were arrested, per the Human Rights Activists News Agency.
According to Iran Human Rights Monitor, Amini suffered severe physical beatings during her arrest. She was subsequently held in isolation in the security ward of Vakilabad Prison in Mashhad for nearly three months.
She remained in administrative and judicial limbo for eight months, deprived of basic rights guaranteed to detainees, the rights monitor said.
CHARGES THAT SEALED AMINI’S FATE
Amini was produced before the Mashhad Revolutionary Court in August and faced several charges, including Moharebeh (enmity against God), Sab al-Nabi (insulting the Prophet), cooperation with a hostile state (Israel), insulting the Supreme Leader, and clashing with security and state personnel.
The charges of Moharebeh and Sab al-Nabi proved decisive, as both offences are punishable by death under Iran’s Islamic penal code.
Citing the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, UK's The Guardian reported that Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends. Her defence argued that the remarks were a "slip of the tongue".
The presiding judge rejected the defence, reportedly asking, "Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?"
In a separate case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison.
Iran Human Rights Monitor said she was denied access to a lawyer of her choice throughout her detention and legal proceedings. She may also have been subjected to physical and psychological torture to extract confessions by force.
'REMEMBER MY NAME'
In an audio recording released from prison last month, Amini appealed for international intervention, urging the United Nations, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.
"I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice," she said.
"I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams," Amini said. "I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning."
"Remember my name; I may not be able to speak again. But as long as I am alive, I hold one hope: that before the rope marks the end of my life, I see my prosperous and free Iran."
Rights groups have warned that Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent.
According to Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out in Iran this year.

articles.title: India’s demographic dividend and the jobs challenge - Daily Pioneer
articles.summary: India’s demographic dividend and the jobs challenge  Daily Pioneer
articles.full_text:
Author: D K Singh
India’s young population offers a powerful economic advantage, but numbers alone cannot guarantee prosperity. The real challenge lies in bridging the education–employability gap, creating quality jobs and preparing young people for an economy increasingly shaped by AI and automation
The working-age population, especially the youth among them, is considered a demographic dividend on whom the future of any country’s socio-economic development depends. Recent youth protests across South Asia, however, have raised a deeper question: Are there enough opportunities to make the youth employable and keep them gainfully employed? If not, then what should be done?
First things first. India, with a population of more than 1.4 billion, has a substantial opportunity: people aged 15-59 are projected to number more than 98 crore and make up nearly 65 per cent of the population by 2030, according to the Economic Survey 2025-26. But a large working-age population becomes an economic dividend only when people can find productive work, earn rising incomes and improve their lives. A large working-age population gives India an important economic opportunity. But numbers alone do not create prosperity. The opportunity must be converted into higher productivity, better incomes and sustained economic growth.
Population becomes a demographic dividend only when people can find productive work, use relevant skills and earn decent incomes. That requires good education, appropriate skills, productive enterprises and enough quality jobs. But the hard economic reality is that quality jobs are not forthcoming. A number of employment surveys vouch for that. In August 2026, the latest monthly Periodic Labour Force Survey available, 52.8 per cent of people aged 15 and above were employed and the labour force participation rate was 55.6 per cent. The unemployment rate was 5 per cent, which means millions are actively hunting for jobs but are out of work, which results not only in the denial of opportunities for people to participate in the economy and find work that uses their abilities but also in a lack of trust in the entire governance process, turning these job-hunters into “cockroach-protesters”.
Young people’s protests
The employment challenge is visible not only in official data but also in protests over examinations, recruitment and jobs. Recent protests across South Asia, including in Bangladesh and Nepal, have reflected young people’s frustration over jobs, opportunity and governance. In India, recruitment delays, examination cancellations and alleged irregularities have also brought aspirants onto the streets. In 2022, railway recruitment protests in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh followed a process in which around 12.5 million candidates applied for roughly 35,000 posts. In 2025, SSC aspirants in Delhi protested over examination glitches and other concerns. More recently, protests in Jharkhand have focused on delays and disputes over state recruitment examinations.
These protests do not speak for every young person. But they point to the anxiety created when candidates invest years preparing for examinations and then face delays, cancellations or uncertainty. For many, public-sector recruitment represents stability and social mobility; a stalled process can mean lost time, income and opportunity.
From skilling to employment
India has made significant progress over the past decade in building a national skilling system. Since Skill India launched in 2015, the government has expanded vocational training, Industrial Training Institutes and apprenticeships through various programmes. By October 2025, more than 1.64 crore candidates had been trained and certified under PMKVY, and 49.12 lakh apprentices had been engaged through NAPS. These programmes have created a valuable foundation. Apprenticeships let young people learn in workplaces, while vocational education offers alternatives to a conventional university degree. The Economic Survey notes that only 4.9 per cent of young people aged 15-29 had received formal vocational or technical training in the data it cites. Skill development programmes, however, must move up now to the highest levels, such as space technology, and be open to all, irrespective of degrees.
Artificial intelligence: disruption and opportunity
Artificial intelligence is already changing work, even as its longer-term employment effects remain uncertain. In the United States, employers announced plans to cut 1.2 million jobs in 2025, with AI cited for 54,836 of those cuts. Salesforce said it had reduced its customer-support workforce from 9,000 to 5,000 after deploying AI agents. Amazon announced plans to cut 14,000 corporate roles as part of a broader restructuring. These examples show how companies are using AI to reorganise work, though not every job cut can be attributed to AI alone.
For India, the challenge is to help workers adapt and use AI to raise productivity. AI tools can support healthcare workers, farmers, small businesses and public services, while creating demand for people who can build, maintain and apply them. The government’s IndiaAI Mission is intended to strengthen the country’s AI ecosystem, and NITI Aayog has outlined a roadmap for expanding AI-related jobs and has estimated that India’s technology and customer-experience sectors could create up to four million new jobs in five years.
AI could also help older adults return to work or extend their careers. With suitable training and flexible, remote work, some could contribute to areas such as app development, software testing, digital services and mentoring. This would make better use of their experience while helping them keep pace with changes in the labour market.
A talent dividend
India’s demographic dividend will depend on whether the country can turn its large working-age population into a skilled, productive and fairly employed workforce. That requires not only training, but reliable recruitment, stronger pathways from education to work, and good jobs across sectors and age groups. The test is whether young people can see a credible path from effort to opportunity-and whether workers at every stage of life can participate in the economy. Job-led growth ensuring social mobility of its citizens is the main parameter on which the success of any policy and governance process to turn population asset into demographic dividend will and shall be tested.
D K Singh, A Corporate Governance Expert; Views presented are personal.

articles.title: Why is Marco Rubio skipping Delhi for Mumbai and Reliance hub Jamnagar? What it signals about India-US ties under Trump - Livemint
articles.summary: Why is Marco Rubio skipping Delhi for Mumbai and Reliance hub Jamnagar? What it signals about India-US ties under Trump  Livemint
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s upcoming India visit is drawing attention for an unusual itinerary: Mumbai and Jamnagar, rather than New Delhi, the national capital which is the traditional centre of high-level diplomatic engagements.
The choice of destinations has raised questions about the agenda of the visit and what it signals about India-US ties under President Donald Trump.
The US State Department has said the visit will focus on strengthening the strategic partnership, discussing regional and global developments, and exploring opportunities to deepen energy cooperation.
This will be Rubio’s second visit to India this year, after attending the Quad foreign ministers’ meeting hosted by External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in New Delhi in May.
The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has confirmed that Jaishankar will meet Rubio in Mumbai on October 20.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has also said the trip will have a stronger business focus, with Rubio expected to meet government officials in Mumbai and representatives of Reliance Industries in Jamnagar.
The itinerary stands out because official bilateral talks with a visiting US secretary of state would ordinarily be expected to take place in the national capital.
Mumbai, India’s financial capital, offers access to corporate leaders and financial institutions, while Jamnagar in Gujarat is home to Reliance Industries’ massive refining complex, owned by Mukesh Ambani.
Rubio is expected to visit the refinery and meet Reliance representatives, according to reports citing the US envoy.
The controversy gathered momentum after Washington announced Rubio’s visit and Gor publicly outlined the plan for meetings in Mumbai.
The Indian opposition questioned why Jaishankar would travel outside the capital to meet the US Secretary of State, arguing that the arrangement departed from established diplomatic practice.
Former diplomat Suresh K Goel described the arrangement as unusual, drawing on his experience in the Ministry of External Affairs. He argued that official visits are generally planned by the MEA in consultation with the visiting government and its embassy, distinguishing formal diplomatic engagements from private programmes.
“With my own experience of such visits in the Ministry of External Affairs, it is very strange that the minister should be going to Mumbai for official level discussions with Marco Rubio,” Goel told LiveMint.
He explained that official engagements are normally coordinated through established diplomatic channels, while private programmes are handled separately.
“Whenever the Secretary of State or the foreign minister visits India on an official visit, the programme is prepared by the Ministry of External Affairs in consultation with the embassy or the government of the USA,” he said.
“Any private programme for which he wants to keep his time away that is left to the embassy. But the MEA knows that this is a private programme and they know the programme because his security is the responsibility of the government of India.”
Goel said that if the MEA had prepared the itinerary, the decision to hold the meeting in Mumbai rather than Delhi would merit scrutiny.
“If the Ministry of External Affairs prepared the programme, I do find it that this meeting was not scheduled earlier in Delhi and that he was going to Mumbai or to Jamnagar. Clearly, the agenda for the meeting was not official talks or anything,” he said.
The government, however, has pushed back against the criticism. The MEA has said that hosting foreign dignitaries in cities outside New Delhi is not unprecedented, particularly when visits involve business and sector-specific engagements. Jaishankar’s meeting with Rubio in Mumbai has now been formally confirmed for October 20.
Beyond the debate over protocol, Rubio’s visit comes at a sensitive point in India-US relations, with trade disagreements and differences over energy policy adding to the challenges facing the partnership.
Goel cautioned against allowing disagreements over trade or the tone of bilateral engagement to overshadow the broader strategic relationship.
“The relationship between India and the USA is very, very important in all respects. And therefore, the government, rather than becoming part of this temperament or trade effect kind of a thing, has to be mature in our dealing and try and see how we can actually conduct the relationship,” he said.
He added that the talks between Rubio and Jaishankar would be important in understanding the rationale behind the meeting’s location.
“From that point of view, the conversations between Rubio and the EM are important and perhaps would explain why the minister would want to go to Mumbai to conduct talks,” Goel said.
Despite current differences, Goel said India remains important to the United States because of its economic potential, democratic institutions and cooperation across multiple sectors.
“India continues to be important for the USA as an economic and democratic partner. After all, if you look at Asia, which is the other democracy which can compare in terms of relationship?” he said.
He pointed to the breadth of cooperation between the two countries, including information technology, defence and professional services.
“The relationship—there are many factors here. There are professionals, there is IT cooperation, there is defence cooperation, there are many areas. So India will continue to be important,” Goel said.
Rubio’s visit will therefore be watched not only for the significance of its Mumbai and Jamnagar stops, but also for whether the discussions help sustain cooperation across trade, energy, defence and technology.

Indian pilot Smit Machchhar who was attacked by his co-pilot aboard a Flydubai flight has recalled how a routine journey turned into a fight for survival, describing the repeated blows to his head, his attempts to call for help and the moments he lost consciousness as the aircraft went into a dive.after he was stabbed by his Omani copilot Hamam Al Hammami who was allegedly trying to crash the plane.
In an exclusive 1st news interview after being stabbed, with Sky News Arabia, Captain Smith Machchhar said there had been nothing unusual about the flight until about two hours after take-off. He was carrying out routine checks in the cockpit when the attack began, initially mistaking the first blow to the back of his head for damage to the aircraft.
Giving out details as he remembered he said, "when I was just in in the checking my computer for the timing and everything, uh suddenly there was a a very hard hit at the back of my head, right here. And uh it was quite hard and felt that it was something which was very strong."
He said he initially thought something had broken off the aircraft's roof and hit him, causing catastrophic damage. Drawing on his training, he tried to regain his composure and check the aircraft's systems. “My thought process went on that track, that oh, there is a big damage in the aircraft which has hit me at the back,” he said.
But within seconds, he realised he was being attacked. “He kept on hitting,” Machchhar said. 
He recalled turning around and realising what was happening, although the impact had severely restricted his field of vision.
“Immediately, I would say in the next few seconds, my vision was restricted to like few inches,” he said, adding that he learnt about the extent of the impact from doctors later.
His first response was to protect himself from further blows. He quickly unbuckled his seatbelt, turned around and tried to block the attack, sustaining an injury to his hand. “At this point, it was very obvious what was going on,” he said.
‘Smith, do something. You can’t die like this’
Machchhar said he immediately tried to get help from another captain who was on board and was expected to operate the return flight. “I was screaming his name and I was trying because the switch was very close to me to open the door. I was trying to just get help in,” he said.
He lost consciousness amid the commotion but remembered managing to open the cockpit door. He could hear shouting as the other crew members confronted the co-pilot. “The door shut immediately after that because he threatened to hit them as well,” Machchhar said.
By then, he was struggling to stay conscious and could feel his strength fading because of blood loss. Soon afterwards, he heard the engine sounds change and felt the aircraft go into a dive. “Since I’ve been flying for such a long time, I don’t have to see the instruments to figure out or hear the engine to know what’s happening,” he said.
Machchhar said he repeatedly drifted in and out of consciousness but realised he had to fight to survive. “There was a moment where I realised and I told myself that, ‘Smith, do something. You can’t die like this,’” he said.
His memories of what happened next remain fragmented. He recalled trying to reach the door, bracing his leg against something and pushing himself forward.
“The next memory that I have is the door’s open and I’m lying between the cockpit and the galley,” he said. He remembered being face down as panic and shouting continued around him.
‘Everyone did their best’
While Machchhar was fighting to survive, another captain took over the controls and helped save the aircraft. “The other thing, how my other colleague who took over the controls and saved the day again is commendable. It’s something that I’ll keep with me till I die,” he said.
Asked what he wanted people to understand about the incident amid speculation over how the plane was saved, Machchhar said everyone on board had done what they could.
“I think everyone in world everyone in world did the best in their capacity to save the day,” he said. The pilot said the first blow continued to haunt him in the days after the attack.
“Immediately after the event, I used to get flashes of the first hit. And trust me, it shook me up for the first few days,” he said, describing how the memory would return suddenly and leave his heart racing.
But what stayed with him most was the determination of those on board. “One thing that I would take away from that day was the determination, the sheer determination of everyone to survive,” he said.
Machchhar said he felt out of danger only when the aircraft touched down in Saudi Arabia. By then, a doctor was attending to him in the galley, while crew members worked to keep him conscious.

Machchhar also expressed gratitude for the medical treatment he received in Saudi Arabia and after being brought back to the UAE. “From the first day onwards, the way I was taken care of, the way I was brought back to the UAE, even the care that I was given in Saudi is something I would never forget in my life,” he said.
Still recovering from the traumatic incident, he said he felt grateful for the care and support he had received over the preceding two-and-a-half weeks.

Conventional international relations theory has long maintained that a state's international agency is a direct projection of factors such as domestic stability, fiscal solvency, and material self-sufficiency. Hence, a nation burdened by escalating external debt, deteriorating law and order, and persistent security issues should logically be relegated to the peripheries of the international order. Yet, Pakistan presents a clear contradiction to such conventional lenses, as it continuously maintains an increasingly prominent role in the international order, which should be disproportionate when factoring in its prominent issues.
Additionally, whilst maintaining concurrent, functional partnerships with mutually hostile global and regional power centres, including Beijing, Washington, Riyadh, and Tehran, the nation has been occupying a pivotal intermediary role in the Iran conflict. In using a strategy of strategic hedging, Pakistan gains financial, military, and diplomatic benefits from global, oftentimes competing powers whilst preserving its sovereignty.
However, this leads directly to a major question: to what extent do such domestic vulnerabilities and international liabilities offset the significant influence and agency gained through strategic hedging in an increasingly multipolar order?
The Historical Roots of Strategic Hedging
Pakistan’s history plays a vital role in understanding its foreign policy. Upon its inception following Partition in 1947, Pakistan confronted severe existential challenges, driven by a profound, fundamental mismatch in conventional military capabilities and industrial output relative to India, which was compounded by unresolved territorial disputes in Jammu and Kashmir. To offset this regional imbalance, Pakistan had subscribed itself to the “Western” bloc in the early Cold War, formally acceding to a number of formal pacts with Washington that enabled Pakistan to secure substantial military and financial aid.
However, this alignment had a divergence in interpretation. Washington viewed these alliances strictly as anti-communist containment mechanisms against the Soviet Union and China, whereas Islamabad viewed them as guarantors of national security against Indian invasions or other violations of sovereignty. This difference in interpretation was prominent when the 1959 Executive Agreement failed to receive US congressional ratification. It was further amplified during the 1962 Sino-Indian War and the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War, when Western powers extended direct military aid to New Delhi and imposed arms embargoes on Pakistan, teaching Pakistani statespersons that total reliance on a single superpower or “bloc” was an unsustainable foundation for upholding sovereignty.
Hence, this disillusionment with prior foreign policy decisions ultimately culminated in a marked shift toward Pakistan’s hedging strategy. In the 1963 Sino-Pakistani Boundary Agreement, the two nations settled borders in Kashmir and laid the foundation for a long-lasting partnership; however, Pakistani diplomacy clearly articulated that relations between Beijing and Moscow were not mutually exclusive. This was exemplified during the late 1960s and 1970s when Pakistan leveraged its diplomatic access to both Washington and Beijing to facilitate US National Security Advisor Henry Kissinger’s covert July 1971 trip to China.
The contingent, warfare-based nature of Western alliances in the early 21st century following the 1971 war, the Soviet-Afghan War, and the War on Terror led Pakistan to expand its economic and strategic partnership with China, culminating in the 2015 launch of CPEC, a Belt and Road Initiative involving over $62 billion in planned infrastructure and energy investments centred on Gwadar.
The Erosion of the International Legal Order
This increase in international influence and agency has been catalysed by the erosion of the post-Cold War unipolar order and the erosion of international legal systems, as the enforcement capabilities of public international law have buckled. A marked breakdown of compliance with International Humanitarian Law, the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and the 1948 Genocide Convention in West Asian conflicts has been observed, and the deep-seated paralysis of international judicial institutions is evident. While the International Court of Justice has issued binding provisional measures of action, it possesses no independent enforcement mechanisms, instead relying entirely on a UN Security Council frequently deadlocked by permanent member vetoes under Article 27(3).
Similarly, political resistance to International Criminal Court arrest warrants further propels the erosion of universal legal norms. For middle powers like Pakistan, this further reinforces the fact that not only historically, but also currently, formal legal commitments offer little to no guaranteed protection for sovereignty, thus incentivising such middle powers to construct alternative security architectures.
 Ultimately, until Pakistan addresses its underlying economic, security, and legal vulnerabilities, strategic hedging is unlikely to provide a stable basis for sustained international influence
Beyond the confines of conventional warfare, the international legal order is further destabilised by the increasing weaponisation of global finance, which directly challenges the principle of non-intervention under Article 2(7) of the UN Charter. Precedents such as the freezing of Venezuelan sovereign wealth and central bank assets, alongside third-party sanctions that bypass World Trade Organization rules, compel middle powers to diversify their financial networks and trade corridors.
Also, the Law of Armed Conflict has been eroded by expansive doctrines of self-defence, where states use subjective interpretations of Article 51, including preemptive self-defence and the unwilling or unable doctrine. This, coupled with maritime threats in key chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, which challenge the transit passage regime under Part III of UNCLOS, and the collapse of nuclear de-escalation agreements like the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, leads middle powers to face an international landscape in which rules-based systems offer minimal protection.
Regional Diplomacy and Economic Manoeuvring
In response to these regional uncertainties, Pakistan has applied its hedging apparatus across West Asia by refusing to subscribe to any single regional bloc. However, the Makkah Pact alongside Saudi Arabia and Turkey, governed by pacta sunt servanda under Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, binds signatories to treat an act of armed aggression against one as an act against all, echoing a NATO-esque defensive clause. Still, the treaty text omits explicit language, creating a calculated sense of ambiguity. Nevertheless, during maritime disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Pakistan invoked the 2006 Preferential Trade Agreement and 2021 Joint Border Trade Agreement with Iran to route commercial trade through overland transit corridors at Taftan and Mirjaveh, displaying the lack of total subscription to any bloc in the Middle East either.
Globally, Pakistan uses strategic hedging to attain economic, military, and technological benefits from both Washington and Beijing without incurring the costs of exclusive alignment. In 2026, during the Donald Trump administration, Pakistan finalised a memorandum of understanding between its Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Defence, and the US General Services Administration to redevelop the historic state-owned Roosevelt Hotel in New York, valued at over $1 billion, into an international asset-restructuring plan to generate foreign currency revenue.
Currently, the Virtual Asset Regulatory Authority has enacted an agreement with US-linked SC Financial Technologies to integrate the USD1 stablecoin into national cross-border payment networks, linking Pakistan to American fintech infrastructure. In the critical minerals sector, Pakistan dispatched its first consignment of enriched rare earth elements to US Strategic Metals under a $500 million agreement with the Frontier Works Organisation. In the defence domain, Washington authorised a $1.17 billion modernisation package for Pakistan's F-16 fleet, including radar contracts with Northrop Grumman Systems. Still, in the 21st century, Pakistan has been able to develop its own JF-17 fighter jets alongside the Chengdu Aircraft Corporation, further exemplifying the non-exclusive nature of its foreign policy. Such agreements build upon the infrastructure established under CPEC, where a decade of Chinese capital funded high-voltage energy grids, development in Gwadar, and localised assembly plants for Chinese electric vehicles.
Furthermore, Pakistan's posture enables it to act as a crucial diplomatic intermediary during major crises, as demonstrated during the early 2026 escalation between Washington and Tehran, as Pakistan maintains a unique degree of credibility in both camps that are at loggerheads. During escalating military exchanges in early 2026 that threatened global energy security in the Strait of Hormuz, Islamabad initiated backchannel diplomacy to facilitate negotiation exchanges under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter. These efforts produced an immediate ceasefire on the 8th of April 2026, known as the Islamabad Accords, followed by Pakistan hosting senior American and Iranian delegations on the 11th of April 2026 for their first direct talks on Pakistani soil since 1979. articles.summary: J-1 probe deals another blow to Indian researchers’ American Dream  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
He is not alone.
Increasingly, Indian researchers are re-examining the US for doctoral and postdoctoral opportunities as a federal probe into exchange visas, research funding cuts, and uncertainty over duration of stay threaten to complicate their academic careers, study-abroad consultants said.
The Trump administration has launched investigations into J-1 exchange visitor visa programmes at nine universities, including Harvard, Stanford and MIT. The visa category covers exchange visitors such as research scholars, professors and postdoctoral researchers.
Also Read | More US universities may face J-1 visa fraud probes, says Labor Department IG D'Esposito
According to Vice President JD Vance and US Department of Labour Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito, the probe examines alleged misuse of visa classifications by these institutions for deploying J-1 exchange visas for federally funded grant research at a rate of 61% (compared to the national average of 38%) and paying foreign researchers roughly $20,000 less than American graduates and researchers.
The investigations come amid research funding disruptions and a proposed change that would replace the existing duration-of-status framework with a fixed admission period, generally capped at four years. A federal court has blocked the change for now, leaving the existing framework in place while litigation continues.
The 2025 Open Doors Report said Indian nationals were the second-largest cohort of international scholars in the US, after the Chinese in the 2024/25 academic year. At 19,156, Indian scholars accounted for 16.4% of the total international scholar population, registering an 8% increase from the previous year, when they numbered 17,735.
Nikhil Jain, founder of ForeignAdmits, said the shift was visible in applicant enquiries at his firm. “Overall PhD enquiries are up, but US PhD enquiries are down more than 40%, even for offers with confirmed funding, while Europe has more than doubled.” He added, “A few people in our own IIT network have deferred US PhD starts this year. Partially funded US PhDs are dropping off shortlists.”
Also Read | US universities review CPT rules for international students as higher education groups seek court relief, hearing on November 6
Jain said postdoctoral researchers and visiting scholars at the nine universities under scrutiny faced the most immediate uncertainty, particularly in biomedical and life sciences research. PhD students on F-1 visas are less directly exposed to the J-1 probe but remain concerned about funding and stay rules.
Praneet Singh, vice president of university partnerships at upGrad Study Abroad, said the uncertainty was pushing applicants towards Europe, particularly Germany, Switzerland and Scandinavian countries, where doctoral programmes are often salaried research positions backed by established funding.
“This has been an especially difficult year for PhD applicants. The US’ new four-year cap on international students’ authorised stay and consistent cuts to research funding have made it a riskier choice,” Singh said, adding that some universities had reduced their doctoral cohorts.
Aditya Shanker Raghuwanshi, founder of Masterclass Space, said families were increasingly weighing the risks of committing several years to research in the US. “The US is still the first choice for most families we meet. They’re just keeping a longer, more serious backup list than they did a year ago.”
Raghuwanshi said funding, the ability to remain in the country long enough to complete a PhD, which often takes five to six years, and employment prospects after graduation were among the biggest concerns. The J-1 probe, he said, had added to the perception that scrutiny of foreign talent was extending beyond students to research laboratories.
An Indian researcher’s primary concern includes “the ability to maintain momentum in their work–obtain a visa, start their studies or postdoctoral appointment, retain funding, and finish their mission in the US,” said Sanjay Laul, founder of MSM Unify.

articles.title: Rubio’s India Visit: Washington Must Learn to Engage New Delhi on Its Own Terms - The Daily Jagran
articles.summary: Rubio’s India Visit: Washington Must Learn to Engage New Delhi on Its Own Terms  The Daily Jagran
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's scheduled visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar between October 17 and 22, 2026, comes at a consequential moment in India-US relations. With trade negotiations unresolved and Washington intensifying pressure over India's purchases of Russian oil, the visit will test whether the Trump administration can reconcile its transactional approach with the strategic importance it attaches to India.
The emphasis on Mumbai and Jamnagar, rather than a scheduled stop in New Delhi, points to the commercial and energy dimensions of the engagement. Yet the larger question is political: can Washington build a deeper partnership with India without expecting New Delhi to subordinate its national interests to American preferences? India recognises the importance of its relationship with the United States. Defence cooperation, advanced technology, investment, supply-chain diversification, and shared interests in the Indo-Pacific provide a substantial foundation for engagement. But strategic convergence does not imply strategic subordination.
India’s foreign policy remains anchored in strategic autonomy, and its partnerships are instruments for advancing national interests rather than ends in themselves.
For Washington, the challenge is to understand that distinction. India is prepared to cooperate closely with the United States, but the terms of that cooperation must reflect Indian priorities as well as American ambitions.
The prolonged negotiations over a bilateral trade agreement illustrate the difficulties confronting the relationship. The framework announced in February 2026 reduced some punitive US tariffs on Indian goods, with rates reportedly falling from levels as high as 50 per cent to around 18 per cent in earlier stages. Yet disagreements over market access, agriculture, reciprocal purchases, and tariff structures continue to impede a final agreement.
Washington’s concern about India’s goods trade surplus reflects the Trump administration’s emphasis on reciprocity. But reciprocity cannot mean that India must accept American demands irrespective of their consequences for its economy. Agricultural sensitivities, industrial development, and domestic employment are integral to India’s political economy, not peripheral negotiating considerations. New Delhi should therefore resist the temptation to conclude an agreement merely to secure short-term tariff relief.
A durable deal must improve market access, encourage investment, and strengthen India’s economic capabilities without creating asymmetric obligations.
The United States, too, must recognise the limitations of tariff diplomacy. Economic pressure may bring negotiating partners to the table, but it cannot guarantee concessions. Excessive coercion risks encouraging India to diversify its markets and supply chains, undermining the very commercial relationship Washington seeks to deepen. The objective should be an agreement based on mutual benefit, not one in which India’s concessions become the principal measure of success.
India’s continued purchases of Russian crude are a major test of strategic autonomy, as Washington seeks to use economic pressure to influence the energy choices of countries trading with Moscow. With President Donald Trump having signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on September 18, 2026, authorising tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from major buyers of Russian energy under specified conditions, Rubio’s visit comes at a particularly sensitive moment ahead of the October 18 deadline.
For New Delhi, energy procurement must remain guided by national security, commercial viability and consumer interests, given Russian crude’s role in diversifying supplies and potentially reducing costs. India has little reason to accept a precedent that allows an external power to dictate its energy mix, while Washington must recognise that diversification requires competitive prices, reliable deliveries and attractive long-term arrangements. Reports of the United States moving towards Russian diesel purchases amid domestic fuel pressures further expose the tensions between geopolitical demands and national interests. The practical way forward is negotiation, including a predictable understanding on sanctions and any applicable waivers, to prevent the dispute from undermining broader bilateral cooperation.
Jamnagar gives the visit a distinctly strategic-commercial dimension, with Reliance Industries’ refining complex, reportedly capable of processing approximately 1.4 million barrels of oil per day, serving as a major hub for global petroleum processing and refined-product exports. Its capacity to handle diverse crude grades makes it central to debates over energy diversification, linking India’s energy security, global oil markets, private-sector investment and American commercial ambitions.
Investment and offtake arrangements associated with the refinery project announced by Trump in March 2026 in the Texas–Brownsville area could further deepen bilateral commercial ties, but Indian investment in the United States reflects India’s expanding economic reach, not an obligation to align with American energy preferences. Similarly, US energy suppliers must compete on price and reliability rather than rely on political pressure to secure market share. Jamnagar thus illustrates the central bargain underpinning India–US energy cooperation: stronger commercial ties are sustainable when they expand India’s strategic choices rather than constrain them.
A persistent difficulty in Washington’s approach is the tendency to equate strategic partnership with political alignment. Cooperation on defence, technology, and the Indo-Pacific is welcomed as evidence of convergence, while India’s independent positions on Russia, trade, and other international questions are sometimes treated as obstacles.
This misunderstands the basis of India’s importance. India’s economic scale, geographical position, military capabilities, and diplomatic reach make it a consequential power in its own right. Its ability to pursue an independent foreign policy is not a flaw in the relationship; it is an essential feature of the country Washington seeks to engage.
The Quad, defence exercises, technology partnerships, and critical-mineral initiatives demonstrate that substantial cooperation can proceed despite disagreements elsewhere. The task is to prevent differences over energy or trade from becoming impediments to progress across the entire relationship.
The objective is neither automatic alignment nor unnecessary distance, but a partnership in which agreement is negotiated rather than presumed. Rubio’s visit offers an opportunity to move beyond the recurring cycle of strategic reassurance and economic pressure.
Rubio’s visit comes at a moment of opportunity and uncertainty. Trade negotiations remain incomplete, the Russian-oil sanctions question is approaching a critical juncture, and both governments have incentives to expand energy investment and commercial cooperation. The Mumbai and Jamnagar engagements could help establish practical pathways forward, but they cannot eliminate the underlying differences in strategic priorities.
India’s rise is changing the terms on which it engages major powers. New Delhi has both the capacity and the incentive to resist arrangements that unduly constrain its choices. Its foreign policy will continue to reflect national interests, economic development, and strategic flexibility rather than an expectation of permanent alignment with any single power.
For Washington, the implication is clear. If it wants greater access to India’s energy market, it must compete commercially. If it wants a trade agreement, it must negotiate terms that recognise India’s economic priorities. And if it seeks a deeper strategic partnership, it must accept that India’s independent foreign policy is part of the relationship, not a problem to be corrected.
India is prepared to work with the United States, but it is not prepared to make the relationship the organising principle of its foreign policy. The more Washington understands this distinction, the greater the prospects for meaningful cooperation. The less it does, the more likely tactical disputes will obstruct strategic opportunities.
Ultimately, a durable India-US partnership will depend not on India's willingness to accept American terms, but on both countries' ability to negotiate as sovereign partners. Washington must recognise that India’s cooperation cannot be taken for granted or secured indefinitely through pressure. It must be earned through mutual respect, credible commitments, and a willingness to accommodate India’s legitimate national interests.
That is the essential message of Rubio’s visit: the future of the relationship will be shaped not by how far India adjusts to Washington’s expectations, but by how effectively the United States learns to engage a rising India on terms that New Delhi can accept.
(Note: The writer is the Vice President at the Observer Research Foundation.)
