articles.title: Why Trump's plan to unleash 'Mother Of All Bombs' may fall flat in Iran - The Times of India
articles.summary: Why Trump's plan to unleash 'Mother Of All Bombs' may fall flat in Iran  The Times of IndiaExclusive: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, sources say  CNNTrump says US may need to strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain  ReutersTrump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters  Al JazeeraTrump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The 'Mother of All Bombs' has the name, the weight and the explosive punch. What it may not have is the right tool for the job the US wants it to do.
Reports of possible US discussions about deploying the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) against Iran have put the giant conventional bomb back in focus. Weighing just under 10,000 kg, it made its combat debut in April 2017 against an Islamic State tunnel complex in Afghanistan, producing the kind of images that cemented its fearsome reputation.
But Iran's most important nuclear and military facilities are not sitting ducks in the open. Many are buried beneath mountains or shielded by reinforced concrete. And the MOAB, despite its enormous explosive power, is an air-burst weapon, not a specialised bunker-buster.
In other words, a spectacular explosion does not necessarily mean a successful strike. Against Iran's deeply buried infrastructure, the bomb's biggest strength could also prove to be its biggest limitation.
A big blast, not a bunker-buster
The central problem is the MOAB's design. Unlike penetrator bombs, which burrow through soil, concrete and rock before detonating, the MOAB is an air-burst weapon that explodes above the surface, spreading a powerful overpressure wave across a wide area.
This makes it effective against personnel and structures in the open, lightly protected infrastructure, cave entrances and exposed military positions. But much of its energy dissipates horizontally rather than downward. While surface structures can be flattened, heavily fortified underground complexes are far more likely to survive.
Iran's most important assets are not housed in vulnerable surface buildings. Many are concealed beneath mountains and protected by reinforced concrete, meaning the MOAB's explosive power may not translate into the ability to destroy the targets that matter most.
An MOAB strike by US may fail to achieve total annihilation or destruction of a target for several key structural, technical, and operational reasons such as inability to penetrate especially in the mountainous terrain with heavy doors which may absorb the blast effect and since the bomb’s lethal over pressure radius could be localised.
Lt Gen KR Rao (retd), Former Director General Artillery
Iran's underground defence
Iran's nuclear programme illustrates the challenge. Since the early 2000s, Iranian planners have anticipated that key facilities could be targeted by American or Israeli air strikes. As a result, they have placed considerable emphasis on underground construction and hardening.
The enrichment facilities at Natanz include underground sections reportedly protected by thick layers of concrete and located roughly 40 to 50 metres below the surface.
Satellite imagery and open-source analysis have also pointed to extensive tunnelling in mountains near the site. Analysts estimate that some sections could lie even deeper beneath the rock. Such depths pose a challenge even for specialised bunker-busting weapons.
A weapon designed to create a blast wave above the surface would have little prospect of destroying these facilities, since mountain rock absorbs and disperses shockwaves.
Iran's wider military doctrine reinforces this strategy. Over the past two decades, Tehran has publicised underground missile depots, tunnel networks, protected command centres, drone facilities and hardened storage sites.
This tunnelling is a direct response to the conventional air superiority of the United States and Israel. By dispersing vital assets beneath mountains and across multiple locations, Iran has sought to blunt precision-strike campaigns. The assumption is that even an adversary that controls the skies would find it extremely difficult to destroy every critical underground installation.
The MOAB does not change that equation because it was never designed to defeat deeply buried infrastructure on a large scale. North Korea, too, has tunnelled beneath mountains to protect key military infrastructure.
Mountains further complicate the task. While blast waves travel freely across open terrain, natural barriers can absorb, redirect and diffuse the energy of an explosion. Even a weapon with the MOAB's explosive power would face limitations against installations hidden inside or behind mountain formations.
Aircraft carrying MOAB faces its own risks
Operational factors also count against the bomb. Unlike many precision-guided munitions that can be carried by fighter aircraft or stealth bombers, the MOAB must be dropped from a specially modified MC-130 transport aircraft.
Transport aircraft are far less survivable in contested airspace than stealth bombers. Before a MOAB could be used against a strategic target in Iran, American forces would probably have to suppress large parts of Iran's air defence network and establish air superiority. That would be a major campaign in itself.
Securing the airspace would take time. Once that was achieved, planners would have a wider range of strike options and would likely favour weapons better suited to hardened underground targets.
Why GBU-57 is better suited
The GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator offers a clear contrast to the MOAB. It was developed to attack deeply buried facilities that conventional bombs cannot reliably destroy.
Where the MOAB relies on blast, the GBU-57 has a hardened casing designed to penetrate layers of rock and reinforced concrete before exploding. American B-2 bombers used it against Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025.
Planning discussions about hardened underground sites have centred on penetrator weapons rather than large air-blast munitions. The reasoning follows a basic military principle: the target dictates the weapon.
Against caves, trenches and exposed positions, the MOAB may be effective. Against deeply buried nuclear facilities protected by mountains, penetrator weapons are far more relevant.
Psychological impact could outweigh military gains
The MOAB's reputation may be disproportionate to its practical military utility. The weapon is designed not only to destroy certain targets but also to intimidate.
Images of an enormous explosion can carry strategic messaging value, as they did after its use in April 2017. This can be particularly important when policymakers seek to demonstrate resolve or deterrence. A MOAB strike could therefore generate significant psychological and propaganda effects, dominating media coverage.
But strategic success depends not on headlines but on outcomes.
If Iran's critical facilities survived an attack involving one of America's most powerful conventional weapons, the Iranian regime could present it as a propaganda victory. Surviving such a strike could allow Tehran to portray its investments in underground defences as vindicated.
Rather than demonstrating overwhelming American power, an unsuccessful strike against hardened facilities could reinforce perceptions of Iranian resilience.
Escalation is another concern. Any operation against Iran would take place amid maritime trade routes, energy infrastructure, proxy networks and missile forces.
If a MOAB strike failed to destroy its intended target, the United States could still face serious retaliation from Iran and its partners. Military planners generally look for a clear relationship between operational risks and potential gains. A highly visible weapon that raises tensions while inflicting limited damage on the facilities that matter most would be difficult to justify.
A mismatch between weapon and target
The MOAB's limitations against Iran come down to a mismatch between the weapon and its intended targets. It was built to produce devastating blast effects over exposed areas, destroy cave complexes and shock an opponent.
Iran's strategic infrastructure has been adapted to withstand precisely these kinds of conventional threats through deep underground construction, mountainous geography, hardened facilities, dispersed networks and extensive tunnelling.
The MOAB could inflict significant damage on selected surface targets, but it would probably struggle to neutralise Iran's most important nuclear and military facilities. Specialised bunker-busting weapons and broader air campaigns offer more credible options for such targets.
The MOAB remains a formidable weapon, but its strengths are poorly matched to the realities of Iran's defensive architecture.

Indians came to Africa as slaves and later as indentured workers. The 2026 Nobel Peace prize winner’s family is part of that history.
Aziz Hassim's The Lotus People, which opens in Durban in 1882, follows the descendants of two Indian emigrants in South Africa. Amitav Ghosh's Sea of Poppies (2008) sets off in 1838 aboard the Ibis, a former slave ship refitted to carry “indentured labourers” from Calcutta to the sugar estates of Mauritius. MG Vassanji's The Gunny Sack (1989) opens with a man in exile from Tanzania going through a sack left to him by his great-aunt, and recovering from its contents the life of his great-grandfather, who came to East Africa from Porbandar by way of Zanzibar. Abdulrazak Gurnah, the Zanzibar-born writer who won the 2021 Nobel Prize in Literature, writes of what Anders Olsson, who chaired the Nobel literature committee, called "a coastal area in and around the Indian Ocean marked by slavery", shaped by a succession of regimes and colonial powers, the Associated Press reported at the time.
Earlier this month, the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to a woman whose own family came from that history.
Navanethem Pillay, an 85-year-old South African jurist known as 'Navi' and a former United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, was honoured "for her efforts to promote peace and international law". She heard the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, in the courtroom where Nazi leaders were tried after the Second World War. She is the fifth South African to win the prize, after Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, and Nelson Mandela and FW de Klerk.
Pillay, who comes from a family of Tamil origin, was born in Durban in 1941. “My grandparents were shipped from India as indentured labourers," she'd said in a 2013 interview in the South African Yearbook of International Law, recalling that they worked on sugarcane plantations and that Mahatma Gandhi had described their lives as little better than slavery.
Her parents were born in South Africa, she said in that interview, and she was the fifth of their eight children. Her father was a bus driver and her mother a homemaker.
Pillay studied law at the University of Natal. In 1967, she became the first woman to start a law practice in South Africa's Natal Province, defending opponents of apartheid and establishing the rights of prisoners on Robben Island, according to a UN biographical note. She went on to serve as a judge and then president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and as a judge at the International Criminal Court, before leading the UN's human rights office from 2008 to 2014. Most recently, she chaired a UN commission of inquiry that concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejected.
Her grandparents were among hundreds of thousands of Indians whom the British Empire moved to Africa as contract labourers in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Together with later migrants, their descendants now number in the millions across the continent, according to estimates by India's Ministry of External Affairs.
Also read: India condemns JD Vance's ‘indentured servants’ remark amid green card curbs
At the Cape
Indians were living in southern Africa long before the first indenture ships. From 1658, when the Cape was a settlement of the Dutch East India Company, until slavery ended in British colonies in 1834, people from India were among those taken there as slaves, according to a 2015 doctoral thesis by Parbavati Rama at the University of the Western Cape, which builds its count from colonial records held in the Western Cape Provincial Archives.
Indenture begins
After Britain abolished slavery in its colonies, it began recruiting workers in India on contracts that bound them to an employer for a fixed period, a system known as 'indenture'. In 1834, the British government chose Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, as the first site for what UNESCO calls the "great experiment" in using indentured, rather than enslaved, labour.
Between 1834 and 1920, almost half a million indentured labourers from India passed through Port Louis, the site of the Aapravasi Ghat immigration depot, to work on the island's sugar plantations or to be sent on to Réunion, Australia, southern and eastern Africa or the Caribbean, according to UNESCO, which made the depot a World Heritage Site in 2006. Other colonial powers adopted the system from the 1840s, and more than two million indentured labourers were moved around the world, UNESCO says.
South Africa's first indentured Indians, bound for the British colony of Natal, came 26 years later aboard the Truro, which reached Natal on November 16, 1860. By the time the last ship, the Umlazi, came in on July 11, 1911, about 152,000 indentured Indians had made the crossing from Madras and Calcutta on 384 voyages, according to ship lists held by the Gandhi-Luthuli Documentation Centre at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
And, the gradual end
The traffic to Natal was the first to be stopped, under pressure from within British India’s administration.
In 1910, the Imperial Legislative Council, the legislature of the colonial Government of India, adopted a resolution moved by the nationalist leader Gopal Krishna Gokhale asking that the Governor-General be given powers to prohibit the recruitment of indentured labour for Natal. The government accepted it, according to the council’s proceedings of March 1912. A telegram from the Governor of Natal to the Secretary of State for the Colonies, dated February 28, 1910, now held by the National Archives of India, noted that the resolution did not amount to an immediate ban.
Indentured emigration as a whole was halted in March 1917 under the Defence of India Ordinances, though a final shipment went to Mauritius in 1925, according to the University of Edinburgh's Coolitude archive.
By 1917, more than one million men, women and children had left India under indenture, most never to return, the historian Brij V Lal wrote in a 2021 book chapter on the system's end.
The Indian government ties its diaspora to that period through Gandhi. The MEA holds Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, its annual day for overseas Indians, on January 9 because Gandhi returned to India from South Africa on that day in 1915.
Also read: Margaret Hamilton, who led Apollo's software team, and the women whose work shaped modern computing
Indian communities today
Today, South Africa has the largest population of Indian origin in Africa, with MEA estimating the total at 1.8 million, 1,722,600 of them people of Indian origin and the rest Indian citizens.
South Africa’s census of 2022 counted 1,697,505 people in its Asian group, a category that accounted for Indians and people of other Asian origins, with 1,157,542 of them in KwaZulu-Natal, the province that includes Durban. But demographers Tom Moultrie and Rob Dorrington, in a 2024 technical report for the South African Medical Research Council, warned that the census probably overestimated the group and that its figures should be used with extreme caution.
Of those counted, 37.1% identified as Hindu, according to Statistics South Africa's 2025 report on cultural dynamics.
In Mauritius, where the 2022 census recorded about 1.24 million residents, MEA estimates 891,697 Indian citizens and people of Indian origin. It puts the figures for Kenya at 80,000, Tanzania at 55,000 and Uganda at 38,800.
Pillay’s pending case
Pillay is serving as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in The Gambia's case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya.
Speaking in Nuremberg on the day of the award, she warned that attempts to weaken international criminal justice "risk returning us to a world in which power, rather than law, determines whose suffering matters".

articles.full_text:
Iran has provided Yemen’s Houthi rebels with intelligence and tactical guidance to help them target Saudi Arabia and forces allied with Riyadh, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal, raising concerns about Tehran’s growing role in the conflict and the threat to regional security.
According to WSJ report, Iranian assistance has extended beyond weapons supplies to intelligence-sharing and operational support. The allegations point to closer coordination between Tehran and the Houthis as the group intensifies its military campaign against Saudi Arabia.
The support the Houthis received from Iran and other Axis actors “undeniably paved the way for the rapid-fire gains they’ve made over the past few months,” Adam Baron, a Yemen expert and fellow at the Washington-based policy institute New America, told the WSJ.
Iran’s assistance reportedly includes intelligence to identify targets, training in operating advanced weapons, tactical guidance and help developing locally manufactured drones and missiles.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Lebanon’s Hezbollah have helped the Houthis acquire technical expertise in missile systems and weapons production, according to experts cited by Reuters.
The assistance is also intended to reduce the Houthis’ dependence on direct weapons shipments from Iran.
Andreas Krieg, a senior security studies lecturer at King’s College London, said, “Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted.”
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch of Israeli defence intelligence, told the WSJ that the operational relationship between Tehran and the Houthis was “very, very strong”.
“Iran has a major interest in the Houthis’ success,” Citrinowicz said, adding that the attacks harm Saudi Arabia and push up oil prices. He described the relationship as one based on “strategic cooperation” rather than a conventional client-patron arrangement.
Iran and the Houthis’ relationship
The relationship between Iran and Yemen’s Houthis developed from shared political interests into a closer military partnership over the past two decades.
The Houthis emerged in northern Yemen during the 1990s as a movement rooted in the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam and began fighting the Yemeni government in 2004.
Iran’s support expanded as Yemen’s political crisis deepened following the 2011 Arab Spring and the Houthis strengthened their position against the government.
In March 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition to support Yemen’s internationally recognised government and push back against the rebels, turning the conflict into a major regional confrontation involving Riyadh and Tehran.
Iran’s military assistance to the Houthis grew during the war, including reported supplies of missiles, drones, training and technical expertise.

articles.title: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to Visit India: Mumbai, Jamnagar on Agenda - Dainik Jagran MP CG

articles.full_text:
Sandeep Patel
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled to visit India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar for strategic, trade, energy and business discussions.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled to visit India from October 17 to 22, 2026, with planned stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar to strengthen bilateral relations, expand energy cooperation and promote commercial investment.
The visit is part of a broader diplomatic trip that also includes Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where Rubio is scheduled to participate in the C5+1 Ministerial meeting with Central Asian countries. The US Department of State announced the itinerary on October 13.
The proposed engagements come as India and the United States continue discussions on trade, energy security, investment and broader strategic cooperation.
Mumbai Meetings to Focus on Strategic and Economic Ties
Mumbai is expected to be a key stop during Rubio's India visit, with discussions focusing on the bilateral strategic partnership, regional developments, energy cooperation and commercial engagement.
Rubio is expected to meet senior Indian officials and business representatives to discuss opportunities for strengthening economic ties and expanding cooperation between the two countries.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has indicated that business engagement will be an important focus of the visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar is also expected to participate in discussions in Mumbai, according to reports published ahead of the trip.
The meetings could provide an opportunity to review ongoing trade discussions and identify areas for closer collaboration in sectors such as energy, technology and investment.
Any new agreements or policy announcements should be reported only after official confirmation.
Jamnagar Visit to Highlight Energy and Investment
Rubio is also scheduled to visit Jamnagar in Gujarat, home to Reliance Industries' major refining complex.
The visit is expected to include engagements with business leaders and discussions on energy cooperation, commercial investment and opportunities for greater economic collaboration.
Energy remains an important component of India-US relations. Both countries have interests in strengthening commercial ties, improving energy security and expanding investment opportunities.
The proposed Jamnagar engagement also comes amid ongoing discussions about tariffs, trade policy and India's purchases of Russian oil.
Although the visit could provide an opportunity to discuss these issues, no specific investment commitment or bilateral agreement should be assumed before an official announcement.
Rubio's Second India Visit in 2026
The scheduled trip will be Rubio's second visit to India in 2026. He previously travelled to New Delhi in May for a Quad Foreign Ministers' meeting hosted by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar.
The Quad brings together India, the United States, Japan and Australia to discuss regional cooperation and security issues in the Indo-Pacific.
Rubio's latest trip is expected to combine diplomatic engagements in Central Asia with meetings in India focused on strategic and commercial relations.
Uzbekistan Visit to Precede India Engagements
Before travelling to India, Rubio is scheduled to attend the C5+1 Ministerial meeting in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
The C5+1 framework brings together the United States and five Central Asian countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
The meeting is intended to advance cooperation on regional security, economic development and other shared priorities.
A US commercial delegation comprising more than 200 business leaders is also expected to participate in the Central Asian leg of the trip, according to the supplied reporting.
The Uzbekistan and India engagements form part of a wider effort to strengthen US diplomatic and commercial relationships across strategically important regions.
What to Watch During Marco Rubio's India Visit
Several developments will be worth monitoring during the scheduled visit:
- Mumbai meetings: Discussions with senior Indian officials on bilateral relations and regional developments.
- Trade negotiations: Any announcements concerning tariffs, market access or progress towards a trade agreement.
- Energy cooperation: Potential developments involving energy security, commercial supplies and investment.
- Jamnagar engagement: Discussions with business representatives and Reliance Industries.
- Investment announcements: Any confirmed commercial commitments or agreements arising from the visit.
- Regional diplomacy: Outcomes from the C5+1 Ministerial meeting in Samarkand.
The significance of the trip will depend on the discussions held and any formal announcements made by the governments or participating businesses.
Conclusion
Marco Rubio's scheduled India visit from October 17 to 22, 2026, is expected to focus on strengthening strategic relations, expanding commercial engagement and advancing energy cooperation.
Mumbai is expected to host diplomatic and business discussions, while the planned Jamnagar stop highlights the importance of energy and investment in bilateral ties.
The broader itinerary also includes the C5+1 Ministerial meeting in Uzbekistan, connecting the visit to wider US engagement with Central Asia.
The itinerary and reported engagements should be treated as scheduled plans until confirmed through official updates. Any agreements, investment commitments or policy changes should be reported only when formally announced.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday sharply criticised US President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying it would send cash back to Moscow, and accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of reducing peace negotiations to a “parody”.
Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy said Russia did not want peace and welcomed the prospect of European allies taking a greater role in talks. EU leaders rallied around him after Trump again criticised Ukraine and called its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”. “And now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal,” Zelenskyy said. “This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz . articles.title: Stable Decoupling: Three Tests For Europe In Face Of Chinese Economic Coercion - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Stable Decoupling: Three Tests For Europe In Face Of Chinese Economic Coercion - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
By Tobias Gehrke
Key Takeaways:
- EU leaders must decide this autumn on rules for Chinese goods entering the single market, conditions for Chinese investment, and limits on Chinese suppliers in critical infrastructure, while facing a €1 billion daily trade deficit and the risk of Chinese retaliation via critical minerals.
- Drawing on the U.S. experience, the article argues that Europe can pursue targeted restrictions and stability simultaneously, using trade-defence tools, the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, and the International Procurement Instrument without allowing a narrow deal to freeze broader action.
- On investment, it calls for making more conditions mandatory under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act so Chinese projects generate local value rather than “screwdriver” assembly; on infrastructure, it urges extending high-risk supplier rules beyond 5G through the Cybersecurity Act revision.
This autumn, Europeans must decide on new terms of engagement with China. They are facing a surging EU trade deficit of €1bn a day, industrial deterioration across the continent and Chinese threats of economic coercion.
Trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing this week for the final stretch of trade talks, just as Paris and Berlin publish a joint paper demanding tougher trade action against China. At a European Council summit later this month, leaders will be asked whether they wish to negotiate an agreement with China covering these issues—or whether instead to follow the Franco-German push and move to enforce European interests unilaterally by introducing tougher restrictions on China’s access to the single market.
In weighing this question, Europe’s leaders must settle three decisions: first, what rules to set for Chinese goods to enter the EU; second, what they want Chinese investment to contribute to European industry; and, third, where they should limit the roles of Chinese suppliers in critical infrastructure. Looming over all three choices is the geoeconomic reality that Beijing can retaliate—most critically, by restricting exports of critical minerals products to Europe.
The US experience
Recent US dealings with China offers guidance for how (and how not) to make such choices under threat of retaliation. In 2025, Washington assumed that imposing major tariff hikes would harm the Chinese economy and leave Beijing scrambling to make economic and political concessions. Instead, China responded by expanding restrictions on essential rare earth supplies. This put Western factories and defence production under immediate pressure. It forced the White House to de-escalate its tariff hikes and seek accommodation for a more predictable trade relationship.
Now, Washington is pressing ahead with targeted efforts to limit options for where Chinese companies sell, invest and operate. This includes restricting companies’ access to the US market beyond tariffs, while also curbing investment from China and increasingly banning the use of Chinese technology domestically. Despite China’s potent escalation options, the US is pursuing both stability and decoupling at the same time.
The lesson for Europeans is that talks and bargaining with Beijing can help contain escalation while enforcing their own rules across trade, investment and critical infrastructure.
How the EU navigates its season of decisions will determine whether it can successfully defend its industrial and security interests in the face of China’s threats of retaliation.
Three decisions for the EU
What China sells
Europe’s first decision is whether to accept a narrow trade settlement with China in October. Such a settlement—for example, focused on automotive exports, which the two sides are currently discussing—may ease some tensions. It could see China voluntarily limit the number of electric and hybrid vehicles it sends to the EU each year. Or it could involve expanding so-called “price undertakings” in which individual Chinese producers agree to market entry terms, such as minimum import prices, total volume limits or local investment commitments. Volkswagen Anhui, one of the German company’s China-based joint ventures, already agreed to such terms earlier this year.
However, this approach risks failing to address wider industrial challenges posed by the Chinese system. Sectors other than the car industry are already under pressure from China’s industrial policies, including batteries, wind equipment, robotics, machine tools, chemicals and biotechnologies. But a narrow agreement would leave these areas untouched.
Any deal the EU strikes must therefore address these particular issues and support a level of stability between the EU and China—while also preserving the bloc’s ability to tackle other distortions from China independently.
What the EU should do
Therefore, making a deal on one product cannot become a promise to tolerate distortions impacting on others. In the electric vehicle value chain, Brussels must retain its ability to launch anti-subsidy (and safeguard) investigations in other segments of the chain, like batteries, or sectors outside the scope of a settlement. The European Commission must also make use of the anti-circumvention tools it already has to close gaps created by Chinese producers redirecting exports through different locations or product categories. Unlike the Trump administration’s broad tariffs, trade defence measures calibrated to identified distortions would preserve competition in the single market while removing China’s artificial advantages.
The same logic must apply inside the single market, and Europe must maintain its autonomy to enforce a level playing field. This means the EU should be free to systematically launch and conclude investigations under the Foreign Subsidy Regulation across sectors where Chinese state financing is plausibly distorting competition in the single market. The bloc can also make assertive use of the international procurement instrument across every sector where documented procurement discrimination against European firms exists in China.
Furthermore, the EU must press ahead with upgrading its economic security toolbox, and make sure its contents are not beholden to any deal agreed with China. This includes developing a diversification instrument that could push firms in critical sectors to have a diversified supplier base (this could, for example, work by the EU placing tariffs on overdependent imports). It also means strengthening the anti-coercion instrument to lower the bar for activation, and adding a solidarity fund to compensate companies hit by retaliation and coercion.
Where China produces
Europe’s second decision is about what it expects in return when Chinese companies invest in the single market. Chinese investments in Europe (including Britain) have recovered from a previous lull, reaching almost €17bn in 2025 (nearly a quarter of all Chinese FDI), with 45% of that investment in the automotive and EV sector.
The problem for Europe is that, despite this rising investment, China’s exports are increasing at an even faster pace—supported by continued industrial policy support, persistently weak domestic demand and a weak yuan. Where Chinese investors are active in Europe, the risk persists that they will merely relocate final assembly while their supplier networks and technology remain tightly guarded. Without adequate safeguards, Chinese firms may set up “screwdriver factories” in the EU, which assemble largely pre-manufactured components, while retaining high-value activities in China. Indeed, Beijing has not only instructed its carmakers to follow this path, but also explicitly expanded its control levers to decide which automotive components are allowed for export.
What the EU should do
Europe’s trade and investment policies therefore have to work together. To ensure Chinese investors actually shift production to the continent, Europeans need to change the business arithmetic that makes exporting from China more profitable, whether by imposing tariffs or agreeing a managed trade deal. Where import barriers encourage Chinese investment, the EU must then ensure projects will develop local suppliers and support technology learning or transfer.
The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which is under negotiation, attempts to partially address this issue. Importantly, it marks a shift away from treating foreign investment in batteries, electric vehicles, solar power and critical raw materials as an automatic benefit. Under the plans, investments above €100m would have to meet four out of six conditions intended to generate industrial value in Europe (including introducing ownership limits, a joint venture condition, intellectual property sharing, local sourcing and more). Yet, as currently drafted, the only mandatory condition for foreign investors is to commit to local employment. The proposed design would create an à la carte system in which investors could avoid the requirements that are most important for supporting Europe’s industrial transition and scale-up.
It now falls to member states and the European Parliament to make more investment conditions mandatory if China wishes to enter Europe’s strategic industrial base. They should also future-proof the Industrial Accelerator Act by explicitly allowing the legislation to cover other sectors at the core of industrial competition, such as industrial robotics, wind equipment and medical technology.
What China controls
Europe’s third decision concerns where it allows Chinese suppliers a role in critical infrastructure and systems—and where they are excluded. Member states have in recent years strengthened their foreign investment screening powers and adopted a common approach to high-risk 5G suppliers. Yet the security risks today extend beyond these tools and sectors. They reach deep into European ports, energy systems and connected infrastructure.

As Rubio Lands in India, the U.S.-India Relationship Is Stronger Than It Looks
Despite public disputes over trade and immigration, the strategic partnership’s foundations remain sturdy.
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to India, the U.S.-India relationship appears to many to be facing another cycle of volatility. Trade negotiations have plateaued, disagreements over Russia have intensified, public criticisms have sharpened, and public opinion of the United States has hit a record low in India. Washington’s weaponization of trade and its handling of regional crises have revived doubts about American reliability, while New Delhi’s intransigence on a trade deal, sustained embrace of Russia, and renewed engagement with China have revived India skepticism for some in Washington.
However, beneath the public disputes, the two countries continue to deepen functional cooperation on defense-industrial relations, space, AI infrastructure, and maritime operational security. Despite the downturn, the partnership retains the ability to work together on critically important issues.
This contradiction may have a simple explanation. Failures are public, politically salient, and often immediately apparent, but successes are often hidden from view, highly technical, or take years to materialize. Consequently, perceptions of the political relationship have deteriorated faster than its strategic foundations.
Real Turbulence
This period of turbulence largely began over trade, and the two governments remain divided over market access, tariffs, and India’s purchases of Russian oil. These economic disputes reflect a deeper geopolitical divergence: Washington (and Brussels) increasingly regard Moscow as an active threat to the European security order, and the latest round of U.S. sanctions legislation has caught New Delhi in the crossfire. In contrast, India views Russia through the lenses of energy security, legacy arms dependence, and strategic flexibility, and it bristles at the West’s censure, which it sees as hypocritical.
Significant shifts in U.S. legal immigration policy have also stressed the relationship. The crackdown by President Donald Trump’s administration on Indian technology firms days before a White House delegation travels to New Delhi to revive technology partnerships—under the TRUST Initiative—raises questions of policy coherence.
The past year of U.S. foreign policy has also strained the relationship. Indian officials have criticized renewed U.S. engagement with Pakistan as lacking empathy for India’s counterterrorism challenges, and the war with Iran has created severe economic pressures on India, forcing New Delhi to revert to higher levels of Russian oil imports. Furthermore, the United States’ courtship of China has revived Indian fears of a so-called G2 bipolar world that could constrain India’s rise.
Such disagreements affect public expectations about how each country might behave in a future crisis. Once confidence begins to decline, every dispute risks becoming evidence of a larger betrayal.
Quiet, Banal, Strategic Progress
Focusing on politically salient tensions obscures the steady, often overlooked advances that constitute a major strategic upgrade for the two sides.
Despite the sound and fury of new tariffs, U.S.-India trade grew by almost 12 percent in 2025 to a new peak of nearly $240 billion, with the United States remaining India’s top export destination.
Technology cooperation has also been quietly growing. Take the NISAR satellite, which collects data on changes in Earth’s land, ice, water, and vegetation. Its launch in 2025 was the culmination of a decade of collaboration between two complex bureaucracies—NASA and the ISRO—that successfully overcame regulatory hurdles and political transitions to deploy cutting-edge radars to space.
Another example is AI. Major U.S. technology companies pledged nearly $68 billion in AI infrastructure investments in India last year. The opening of semiconductor corporation Micron’s first assembly and test facility in India on February 28 served as a landmark fulfillment of a 2023 commitment, but it was drowned out by the launch of U.S. Operation Epic Fury against Iran. A few weeks ago, Applied Materials and Lam Research announced their own investments in India’s semiconductor ecosystem.
The defense relationship has proved especially durable. This year, the United States and India are on pace for a record number of joint exercises, including one that involved multiple days of combined air assault operations and Indian and U.S. troops working together at a uniquely granular level just 30 miles from the India-China border. The new ten-year framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership calls for closer coordination across advanced domains, expanded information-sharing, more complex exercises, and deeper defense-industrial ties.
The maritime dimension is particularly consequential. For all the hand-wringing in Washington about the Indian Army’s dependence on Russian arms, the Indian Navy has acquired an array of interoperable U.S. platforms for maritime reconnaissance: P-8 maritime patrol aircraft, MH-60R anti-submarine warfare helicopters, and MQ-9B high-altitude, long-endurance surveillance drones. All are designed to enhance India’s burden-sharing in the Indian Ocean while complementing U.S. naval strategy in the broader Indo-Pacific—including a new Quad initiative for Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration. Behind closed doors, Indian officials routinely talk about joint tracking of Chinese submarines. There is also far too little appreciation of India’s growing role in the U.S.-led Combined Maritime Forces—the first time India has joined a military coalitional effort outside the UN framework.
Hidden Signals
Some of the most consequential achievements—especially in India’s advanced undersea and space domains—remain invisible amid the din of political disputes. For instance, American capital, technology, labs, and accelerators have supported India’s space, semiconductor, and digital ecosystems. However, these connections remain confined to private relationships between firms and, even when publicized, are rarely presented as broader evidence of strategic interdependence.
In other instances, cooperation is deliberately concealed. During India’s 2020 border crisis with China, Washington played a significant role in expediting equipment, gear for extreme cold weather, and intelligence support, but India requested that this all be kept quiet. Beyond indirect assistance, when India leased contractor-owned, contractor-operated MQ-9B Predator drones to surveil its maritime approaches and border with China, it likely relied on former U.S. military pilots to operate those drones on behalf of the Indian Navy from an Indian military base. A couple of years later, U.S. intelligence support likely helped the Indian Army interdict a Chinese army gray-zone probe, but this was never acknowledged.
These episodes suggest Washington can be reliable in a serious security crisis, but that information has gone largely unobserved by the Indian public and many within the Indian government. Indian leadership has concealed these facts to manage escalation, and Washington has respected New Delhi’s preference for discretion, even though the secrecy meant a missed opportunity to deepen trust.
The United States is also guilty of passing up opportunities to spotlight strategic breakthroughs. For example, the full details of the 2025 U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership framework have yet to be made public. This secrecy has consequences: Investors hold back on big bets, export controllers act with excess caution, and lawmakers discount the trade-offs when they choose to enact sanctions, solidifying a strategic ceiling for the relationship.
Delayed Results
Long delays between commitments and delivery compound the visibility problem. Political leaders seek clear results on marquee defense or technology projects within an electoral term, while bureaucracies may take years to turn announcements into contracts and capabilities.
Some of this is the normal lag that occurs when two governments reconcile different acquisition systems, export controls, and technology expectations. India took four years to implement the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness after its announcement in 2022. Some of the MQ-9B Predator drones cleared for sale in 2017 during Trump’s first administration were not contracted until the end of former president Joe Biden’s administration and will be delivered to India around the time the next U.S. administration takes office in 2029. Such lags are hardly unique to the U.S.-India relationship: India’s BrahMos missile joint venture with Russia took more than ten years from initial agreement to induction of the missile, and nearly thirty years later, India has still not fully indigenized the missile.
These delays are also partially the fault of the rigid Indian defense acquisition process. articles.full_text:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar is set to host US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Mumbai on October 20 to advance the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, with key discussions expected on trade, defence, and emerging technologies.
Key Points
- External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar will meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Mumbai on October 20.
- The talks aim to bolster the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, covering energy, trade, defence, and emerging technologies.
- Rubio's visit also includes attending celebrations for the 250th anniversary of US Independence as a Guest of Honour.
- Discussions will also focus on the progress of the proposed India-US bilateral trade agreement, which both sides are close to concluding.
- The MEA clarified the choice of Mumbai for the meeting, citing a practice of hosting foreign dignitaries outside Delhi.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will hold talks on October 20 in Mumbai to bolster the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, with discussions expected to cover energy, trade, defence, critical and emerging technologies and several other key areas of bilateral cooperation.
Key Agenda For India-US Talks
Ministry of External Affairs Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, during his bi-weekly media briefing, was asked if Jaishankar will be meeting Rubio during his upcoming visit to India, the agenda of the meeting, and why Mumbai has been "chosen" for it.
"On October 19-20, 2026, the external affairs minister will host in Mumbai the deputy prime minister and the foreign minister of the UAE, His Highness Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, for an official visit. On October 20, the external affairs minister will hold talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and attend the celebrations of the 250th anniversary of the Independence of the United States as a Guest of Honour," he said.
The forthcoming visit of Secretary Rubio will provide an opportunity for both sides to review India-US relations and discuss ways to "further strengthen our Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership that we have with the United States," the MEA spokesperson said.
Discussions are expected to cover key areas of bilateral cooperation including energy, trade, investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies and other areas of mutual interest, he added.
The two sides will also exchange views on regional and global developments.
"The visit will provide an opportunity to sustain the high-level engagement between the two countries and advance our shared priorities," Jaiswal said.
Why Mumbai Was Chosen For High-Profile Meetings
On the meeting taking place in Mumbai, the MEA spokesperson said it has been the practice in the last decade or so that "we have hosted foreign dignitaries outside Delhi".
"To give you some examples, the Prime Minister hosted the Prime Minister of Spain in Baroda (Vadodara). He hosted Chancellor Merz in Ahmedabad. Prime Minister of Mauritius was hosted by him in Varanasi, and then the external affairs minister hosted the foreign ministers' meeting in Goa. He hosted the foreign minister of Botswana at Kevadia, Gujarat, and the external affairs minister also hosted the Heart of Asia conference in Amritsar," he said.
So that was just to give a few examples of such meetings that have happened outside Delhi, he added.
Clarifying Rubio's Visit Details
During an interactive session at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum here on Thursday, US envoy Sergio Gor said that Rubio will meet Indian government officials in Mumbai and "we expect that minister Dr S Jaishankar will be there".
His comments had created a flutter online and also drew a sharp response from Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, who on Friday questioned the government over Secretary Rubio's proposed meeting with Indian government officials in Mumbai next week, claiming that officials of the MEA were "confused" over it.
He also said Prime Minister Narendra Modi may want to explain the matter.
The US secretary of state will travel to India next week to further strengthen energy cooperation, the Department of State said on Tuesday.
Rubio will first visit Samarkand in Uzbekistan and then travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar in India from October 17-22, it had said.
Gor on Thursday also said Secretary Rubio's upcoming visit to India will be a little more business-focused and he will meet "some of the folks" at Reliance during a trip to Jamnagar in Gujarat.
Advancing India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement
On the proposed bilateral trade agreement between India and the US, Jaiswal said both sides "remain engaged for early conclusion" of this pact, and referred to the remarks in the last two days by the external affairs minister and the Union commerce minister on its progress.
The two sides continue to engage to iron out differences on the proposed deal, and negotiations are heading towards a "landing point", Jaishankar had said at an earlier session at the Bloomberg New Economy, noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remained unchanged.
Gor on Thursday had said negotiations for a bilateral trade deal were moving at an "incredible pace", and the "big items are done", underlining that he was confident that both sides will get the pact through.
During an interactive session at the Forum here, Gor had also echoed Jaishankar's assessment of the progress in the proposed India-US trade pact, saying "we are very close to landing it".
Parallel Diplomatic Engagements In Mumbai
On the visit of the UAE deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Jaiswal said it will be "an opportunity to review all facets of bilateral cooperation under the India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The two delegations will assess and take forward the initiatives in the areas of energy, trade, investment, fintech, defence and connectivity. There will naturally be an opportunity also for a detailed exchange on the situation in West Asia, as also on global and other multilateral issues."

articles.title: India’s new national highway projects taken up in April-Sep clock 63 pc jump - Punjab Kesari English
articles.summary: India’s new national highway projects taken up in April-Sep clock 63 pc jump  Punjab Kesari English
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct 16 (IANS) India’s infrastructure sectors, spanning highways, aviation, telecom, ports, and power, recorded robust growth during the first half (April-September) of the current financial year, according to the quarterly update of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s (MoSPI) PAIMANA Performance Monitoring Dashboard.
National Highways awarded for construction rose 62.9 per cent year-on-year to 2,236.3 km during April-September of FY27. This significant increase strengthens the pipeline of highway infrastructure development, paving the way for enhanced connectivity, improved logistics efficiency, and sustained economic growth, the official statement said.
The telecommunications sector recorded a continued expansion of digital infrastructure, with the cumulative Optical Fibre Cable (OFC) laid reaching 7,52,113 km by August 2026. This represents an addition of 29,256 km during FY 2026–27 (April–August), strengthening the country’s high-speed digital connectivity infrastructure.
The Ports, Shipping, and Waterways sector recorded continued growth in cargo traffic, with cargo handled at major ports increasing by 7.2 per cent year-on-year to 390.4 million tonnes during FY 2026-27 (April-August). Cargo traffic at non-major ports increased by 1.8 per cent year-on-year to 313.4 million tonnes during the same period. Overall, this growth reflects sustained cargo movement and continued utilisation of port infrastructure supporting domestic and international trade.
Indian Railways strengthened its capacity, with the number of coaches increasing by 4.5 per cent and locomotives by 6.4 per cent in FY 2024–25.
The power sector sustained strong growth, with installed capacity rising to 5,32,739.7 MW in FY 2025–26, representing 12.1 per cent year-on-year growth.
The civil aviation sector continues to support India’s growing international tourism footprint, with 30.49 lakh foreign tourist arrivals recorded up to August in FY 2026-27, registering a 2 per cent year-on-year growth. This positive momentum reinforces the sector’s role in strengthening international air connectivity, facilitating tourism growth, and enhancing India’s position as a global travel destination.
The Performance Monitoring Dashboard has now been expanded to 184 indicators. This expansion includes the addition of 21 new indicators, significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness of infrastructure performance monitoring.
Quarterly data has also been updated for 41 indicators across the Power, Civil Aviation, Ports, Shipping & Waterways, and Road Transport & Highways sectors, further strengthening the timeliness and comprehensiveness of infrastructure performance monitoring.
Quarterly updates provide public access to the latest infrastructure performance statistics through a single platform, with sector-wise narratives highlighting key trends across selected indicators.
–IANS

articles.title: Prolonged Political Protests in India: How sustained agitations threaten internal security and national development - Organiser
articles.summary: Prolonged Political Protests in India: How sustained agitations threaten internal security and national development  Organiser
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: Political protests in India are a legitimate public expression of dissent or opposition against a law, policy or action of the government. Though protest is not specifically mentioned in the Constitution of India, it is assured through Article 19, Article 21 and Article 32 of the Constitution. But such a fundamental right is not absolute, and the government under Article 19(2) and 19(3) can impose reasonable restrictions to protect the sovereignty and integrity of India, maintain public order and to prevent defamation/incitement to an offence. In short, our Constitution protects peaceful protests as a democratic right but not at the cost of other people’s right to move, work or live.
Political protests are not new to India, but these protests have increasingly acquired an agitational mode in the last seven years. It started with anti-CAA protests in December 2019, where communal polarisation was attempted, which ultimately resulted in the Northeast Delhi riots in February 2020. It was no coincidence that the riots took place just prior to President Trump’s visit to Delhi on 24-25 February 2020. Farmers’ protests from November 2020 to December 2021 again took a violent turn. Manipur has witnessed violent unrest from May 2023 onwards. Sixth Schedule agitation in Ladakh from the year 2024 onwards is still fresh in our memory. It may be noted that all these protests took place after the NDA coalition under PM Modi returned to power with an even bigger majority in May 2019.
But the protests by Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) against examination paper leaks in June-July this year have added another dimension to the agitational culture in India. The ability of the CJP to mobilise thousands of supporters has surprised the local administration. These organisations have also displayed scant regard for the constitutional bodies. They have exploited social media in a clever manner and have also shown political ambitions. That is why they have started questioning the S.I.R. process and have cast aspersions on the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC). The guerrilla tactics of the CJP have now been adopted by the political opposition in India. That is why the political opposition did the unthinkable act of marching towards the Supreme Court of India in a typical agitational procession.
It is therefore important to understand as to how such prolonged protests and agitations affect the internal security of India. It starts with erosion of trust in the constitutional authorities and important bodies, such as the Supreme/High Courts, ECI, ED, CBI, CAG, RBI, SEBI, etc. Some of the organisations and political parties even question the armed forces. Their aim is to weaken the public confidence in the impartiality of these important functionaries, without any substantive proof. The prolonged agitation over the S.I.R. is simply to disrespect the popular mandate and create confusion in the minds of the people. The S.I.R. process is tedious but critical to cleanse the electoral rolls. Even with the best intentions, some voters may be left out. That is why the ECI has now commenced a special drive to include the left-out voters. But it has to be understood that in a country with approximately 100 crore voters, some anomalies in the electoral rolls are possible.
It is not difficult to see that the prolonged agitations require preventive deployment of the police and paramilitary forces in large numbers. Since these protests happen under the media glare, the law enforcement agencies have to deploy more manpower for crowd control, traffic management and protection of the sensitive installations like the Parliament or the Supreme Court of India. Such regular protests on the streets divert police from crime prevention, counter-terrorism, border policing and community policing. The police are also constrained to restrict the movement of people to prevent untoward incidents. The police are made to look oppressive in the eyes of the people by the leaders leading the protests. In the long term, it creates a sense of mistrust in the law enforcement agencies, as it happened in the case of Manipur.
Two consequences of prolonged protests and agitations weaken internal security, either directly or indirectly. The first one is radicalisation and polarisation. When such protests get amplified through social media, the radical elements take over and polarise the thought process of the innocent public. In the October protests in Delhi, there are credible inputs of Pakistan-sponsored social media handles trying to foment internal unrest in India. The second consequence of prolonged unrest is disruption of essential services, commerce, education, healthcare and ease of movement. There are frequent calls for bandhs, and the common man suffers the most. These disruptions ultimately adversely impact the economy, particularly in the medium and small sectors. A good example of this is the state of West Bengal under the previous Communist and TMC rule. West Bengal witnessed maximum illegal immigration from Bangladesh over the last two decades, because the state became a fertile ground for continuous agitations.
There is another danger. India has just finished Naxalism, and the security forces are now carrying out operations to neutralise the last remnant of the cadre and their hidden cache of arms, ammunition and explosives. My fear is that continued unrest may embolden the urban Naxals to revive Naxalism in India. The government is trying its best to revive the economy in the interiors of Naxal-affected areas. But a false narrative and foreign interference can undo decades of hard work put in by the security forces. I suspect that there would be attempts to cause unrest in the states impacted by Naxalism. The aim of the forces inimical to India’s interests would be to tie down the police and paramilitary forces in unnecessary crowd management, thus weakening the anti-Naxal operations.
Another worrying pattern is giving open threats to the constitutional bodies, law enforcement officials and other government officials that we will sort you out once we come to power. Such an attitude creates a defensive approach from the civil servants and other government officials, including the police. With the threat of a future vendetta, the officials hesitate in taking firm and uncomfortable decisions to maintain public order. Such threats can also lead to politicisation of the government officials, particularly when they are told that more than 200 officials are in touch with the opposition. Therefore, a threat of punitive action against the government officials who are doing their lawful duty has long-term implications for eroding governance. In the Indian context, weak governance invariably impacts internal security.
The legal framework also has to recognise the new realities of the simmering tension and unrest. As the ongoing student movement in France has shown, such protests end up in violence. Thus, the courts have to put reasonable restrictions on protests to ensure public order. The police have a tough job at hand, and they need good SOPs to deal with the unruly mobs. The police also need high-quality training and competent leadership to direct action when necessary. The courts have to consider institutional fatigue, and one odd police aberration should not defame the police. At the same time, the government should not shy away from any administrative correction. A good example was the repeal of the Farm Laws by the Modi government in November 2021.
For a country of 140 crore people and an aspirational society, internal security is the foundation of growth, development and prosperity of the nation. India is aspiring to be a developed nation by the year 2047 @ Viksit Bharat 2047. As we have seen in the past, India’s fragile internal order was exploited by external forces. Modi government has dealt with the internal security threats in a firm manner, be it J&K, the North East and Left-Wing Extremism. India has also articulated a new normal to deal with terrorism sponsored from across the borders. Now the inimical forces have found a new weapon in prolonged protests to weaken the government, both at the centre and in the states, particularly the border states. Repeated attempts by Pakistan to smuggle drugs and war-like stores through drones in Punjab and Rajasthan are another example of how internal security is disturbed. During such a state of perceived unrest in the country, even Elon Musk seeks entry of Starlink into India, disregarding the security concerns and quickly finds support from the LoP.
It is also a fact that external agencies fund, directly or indirectly, many of the agitations in India. Even internal funding is not a problem now. We also find that many such organisations and their leaders are represented by the celebrity lawyers. Many of these lawyers are able to exert pressure on the courts to seek favourable decisions. These brazen acts embolden the fence-sitters, and the agitations tend to persist and broaden. The regime change in India’s neighbourhood (Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh) has also inspired the fringe elements, and we also hear of regime change in India in the ongoing agitation. Such a narrative has extremely dangerous connotations for defending the constitutional order through constitutional means. For the sake of the country, all the stakeholders have to exert themselves to preserve the idea of India. The constitutional bodies have to exhibit transparency and fairness, the courts have to protect the law, and policing has to be firm but impartial. A timely political dialogue and community engagement should find solutions to the genuine grievances of the people. India can not afford to slip away from the growth trajectory through the stage-managed internal frictions.

articles.title: China’s Strategic Reassessment of India - War on the Rocks
articles.summary: China’s Strategic Reassessment of India  War on the Rocks
articles.full_text:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
As China and India have improved their relations in recent months, many observers have attributed this improvement to the end of U.S. strategic altruism toward India. Indeed, in the past year, China has watched India lose its balance and simmer in a sense of strategic disorientation due to America’s change of heart. Delegation after delegation of Indian strategists visited China, trying to mend ties in search of balance in the Chinese view. Many Chinese experts see India as returning to middle-power alignment for “economic authority and strategic freedom,” which translates into vigorous outreach to Europe, Japan, Canada, and all the middle powers. It’s almost as if India is returning to its middle-power roots.
The Chinese reassessment of India’s power status and its strategic malleability — the extent to which its choices can be shaped — and predictability has significant implications for understanding future dynamics between the two powers. The renewed improvement in ties raises questions about its sincerity and limits. While China recalibrates its relations with India, it is also building fences and chokeholds, first and foremost through supply chain dependence. It is unclear what future policy the next U.S. administration will pursue toward either China or India. Both powers therefore keep their options open.
These assessments reflect ongoing research on China’s role in South Asia. They draw on 10 research trips to China, as well as roundtables and exchanges held online and in Washington with Chinese experts since January 2025. China demonstrates a strong tendency toward binary judgments on India’s alignment choice, while the reality is far more nuanced, as U.S. policy should be.
In the Chinese policy discourse on India, the first and foremost question has always been India’s power status: Is India a great power, or is it simply a middle power with great-power potential? While India’s gross domestic product has consistently been a fraction of China’s, its claim to great-power status has had major sway over China’s calculus. Vishwa Guru — “India the world’s guru” — is a famous slogan created under the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi that, in the Chinese view, best represents India’s strategic aspiration: India not only aspires to be a world-class great power but also sees itself as superior and therefore will teach all the other great powers. Although Chinese policymakers do not have romantic misperceptions of India’s actual power status, India’s aspiration and, even more so, its boldness have been no small shock to Chinese policymakers, who follow the tradition of overestimating adversaries’ capacity and hiding their own strength （料敌从宽，判己从严）. India’s bold statement made Beijing question whether it underestimated fundamental aspects of Indian capability and potential that warranted India’s great-power status.
More importantly, during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration, China stopped questioning India’s great-power status. India played a pivotal role in America’s Indo-Pacific strategy during these eight years, to the extent that Washington “hyped India’s power status” （大肆吹捧印度） and “exaggerated India’s development potential.”（夸大其发展潜力）
America’s willingness to elevate India to a global great power and its seemingly endless provision of assistance to lift India up changed China’s original view that only real comprehensive national power mattered. India’s gross domestic product has been only about 20 percent of China’s and has been unlikely to catch up any time soon to become China’s peer. However, that could entirely change if American support continues. Beijing knows this too well because China had been the beneficiary of similar American support and elevation from the 1970s to the 2000s. The difference for China is that back then the United States supported China to counter the Soviet Union, and during the first Trump and Biden administrations, the United States lent similar support to India to counter China. The lesson for China is that great-power status does not actually have to be expressed in real, current terms rather than future expectations and potentials, and U.S. support could very realistically and rapidly elevate India to a new height and single-handedly make India a new great power.
Seeing India as an aspirational and rising power, China believes it followed a policy of accommodation with India throughout this period and beyond. General Secretary Xi Jinping continued outreach and friendly messaging to Modi, including in 2018 (right after the Doklam standoff in 2017); in 2024 at the Kazan summit of the expanded economic bloc originally formed by Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa; and in 2025 when hosting Modi at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit. China did not pursue reciprocal, retaliatory economic policies toward India after 2020. Even on the issue of visas, Chinese officials cited the 280,000 visas China issued to Indian nationals in 2025 to highlight the 2,000 visas India issued to Chinese nationals during the same period to demonstrate the vastly different treatments. For China, these are all reflections of its unwillingness to completely sour ties with India.
But now, with India losing America’s favor, India’s great-power status has become much less persuasive. Chinese strategists are returning to the view that perhaps, after all, India is just a middle power. It has great potential, but elements in the Indian strategic culture pose irremovable obstacles and consistently sabotage its ascension.
As Chinese strategists observe the fluctuation of ties between the United States and India in the past nine years, it is unsettling and reassuring at the same time. The vast scope and depth of what the United States and India could jointly achieve materially and in practice is unsettling for China, exacerbating China’s anxiety about India’s future alignment or alliance with the United States and how it could undermine China’s roles and aspirations. However, the limitations to what the United States could persuade India to do, even with great rewards and strategic benefits promised, are reassuring for Beijing.
For example, despite the favors and support the United States is willing to provide India, India has refused to abandon its strategic autonomy. At the height of the Russo-Ukrainian War and American demand for India to cooperate, India refused to abandon economic and energy ties with Russia. In private conversations, India’s foreign policy community firmly distinguished between “like-minded” and “same-minded” countries to protect its strategic autonomy, and Indian diplomats vehemently emphasized issue-based alignments rather than permanent, rigid alliances.
For China, this is cognitively incomprehensible, as it essentially equates to “India wants to have its cake and eat it, too.” If the United States does not have full confidence in Indian loyalty and support, why would the United States spend its valuable resources to do India the favor and let India run with its own agenda? If the answer is a shared U.S.-Indian aspiration to curtail China’s rise and expansion, India’s expressed reluctance to support the United States and confront China militarily on China’s western flank in a future Taiwan contingency, a position that was reiterated amply in track two dialogues, has certainly made the case of “strategic altruism” less appealing for the United States.
On the drastically different interpretations of U.S. support and Indian reactions, all of the China and India specialists I spoke with refer to the Indian concept of “Dānā” (almsgiving) to explain what they see as India’s “ungratefulness.” What the United States identified as strategic altruism, India sees as strategic egoism because, in Indian culture, the concept of almsgiving views the recipient as doing a favor to the giver by providing them an opportunity to clear negative karma and practice detachment. Following this logic, Indian acceptance of U.S. assistance is India doing the United States a favor, and the United States should be in debt to India consequently. The correctness of this Chinese argument is debatable, but Chinese specialists’ unanimous claim of this cultural reading of a religious tradition as the origin of Indian strategic behavior is certainly noteworthy.
Essentially, China perceives India’s strategic choice as unmalleable, which significantly, or even critically, undercuts India’s potential. Despite the amount of support the United States was willing to supply, India has adhered to its strategic autonomy and refuses to alienate Russia or support a U.S. military campaign against China. Similarly, despite the amount of accommodation China sees itself as willing to provide India, including in economic cooperation, India also adheres to its longstanding position and refuses to forge closer ties. That means India’s strategic choice is predictable and cannot be shaped by the enticement of rewards or the threat of punishments. That substantially reduces the strategic value of India as a U.S. partner in strategic competition with China, and consequently, China’s anxiety about India’s alignment with the United States. Meanwhile, because of the expected limitation to India’s cooperation with the U.S. on the latter’s competition with China, it also considerably decreases India’s strategic appeal for China to pursue.
Once the strategic questions of India’s power status and its alignment choices are answered, China’s remaining choices concern tactical approaches. With diplomatic engagement and maneuvering ongoing, China is most confident in the supply chain dependence it has built up vis-à-vis India. articles.title: ‘Biggest Hurdle’: Nirmala Sitharaman On Why India Struggles To Sell More Goods In China - Times Now
articles.summary: ‘Biggest Hurdle’: Nirmala Sitharaman On Why India Struggles To Sell More Goods In China  Times Now
articles.full_text:
Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has identified non-tariff barriers as the biggest hurdle in India’s trade relationship with China, warning that restricted access to the Chinese market continues to widen the trade imbalance between the two countries. Speaking at a session with Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council on ‘India’s economic edge’, held alongside the World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Sitharaman said India has consistently raised concerns over the difficulties faced by its exporters. She also stressed that New Delhi prefers negotiations and dialogue over retaliatory trade measures to address such imbalances.
Addressing the challenges in bilateral trade, the Finance Minister said, “So non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China. That is one, and second, if the approach globally that you see today, where imbalance is huge, countries impose tariffs and say, ‘no, we cannot sustain this imbalance, either you correct it or else we are going to be very punitive on you’, that approach we have never taken.”
Sitharaman said the trade relationship continues to be tilted against India, with the imbalance expanding despite years of discussions between the two countries.
“The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking about with China now for several years. We are denied market access, even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China.”
Her remarks underline India's continuing concerns over the limited opportunities available to domestic producers in one of the world's largest consumer markets. According to the Finance Minister, Indian exporters face obstacles even in sectors where the country has established a strong international presence.
Generic Drugs, Agricultural Products Face Market Access Hurdles
Sitharaman pointed to pharmaceuticals and agricultural commodities as areas where Indian businesses could potentially expand their presence in China. However, she said regulatory and other non-tariff restrictions have continued to impede access.
“We are global leaders in generic drugs, bovine meat, vegetables and perishables and very many such goods which have huge potential in China. I would think a decade has gone by, consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products. But non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly, whether it is in the name of phytosanitary measures or any other, for which due investigations can happen, for which due both sides sitting and talking can happen, but no progress is made,” the Minister said.
Phytosanitary requirements are measures related to protecting plant health and preventing the spread of pests and diseases. While such regulations can serve legitimate purposes, Sitharaman argued that Indian exporters have struggled to secure progress on market access despite prolonged engagement.
The Finance Minister also explained why India has not chosen to counter China's restrictions with similar barriers or countervailing duties. She said the government continues to pursue discussions, even when negotiations take considerable time.
“it is not the way India believes in dealing with trade negotiations. We sit and talk. It is sometimes very tiresome. But we do go through that approach rather than put CVDs, countervailing duties or some non-tariff barriers to counter the non-tariff barriers on the other side. So these are ways in which we find it difficult to correct the imbalance which prevails between China and us.”
India-US Trade Agreement
Beyond India's economic relationship with China, Sitharaman discussed the proposed trade agreement between India and the United States, expressing hope that negotiations would conclude soon.
“I think recently, a day or two ago, the Indian Commerce Minister has also spoken that they expect and wish to have the [India-US] agreement signed soon. Negotiations have been going on, I hope, in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners, India and US, the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest,” she noted.
An agreement could shape trade relations between the two economies and provide greater clarity for businesses operating across both markets. Sitharaman's remarks indicate that the government remains keen to make progress on the negotiations.
The Finance Minister reiterated India's commitment to multilateral cooperation while highlighting its efforts to strengthen trade ties through agreements with individual partners.
India is pursuing trade arrangements involving the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Canada and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, alongside negotiations with the United States.
