articles.summary: Iran says two tankers catch fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz  Al JazeeraIran war live: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats; drones target Riyadh  Al JazeeraVideo: Iranian Fishermen Race To Grab iPhones, Perfume From Sunken Cargo Ship  NDTVOil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: Iran's Guards  The Hindu'War booty': Cheap iPhone 18s advertised in Tehran after Hormuz shipwreck, claims report  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said two oil tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
The first tanker hit a mine, triggering an explosion and a “fierce fire”, the IRGC said on Saturday, while the second tanker hit a mine that engulfed it “in a massive blaze”, Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported.
Information about the ships’ names or the origin of their cargo was not immediately available.
IRNA said the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route not authorised by Iran.
The IRGC also claimed that while one tanker tried to cross the waterway “with US support”, the second vessel was left immobilised.
Iran seized control of the Strait of Hormuz after the US-Israeli war on the country began in late February. Tehran has since demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. About one-fifth of global oil consumption transited the waterway before the war.
This week, IRGC naval commander Rear Admiral Ali Azmaei warned that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile”.
The United States has imposed its own naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports.
Iran’s army earlier said that two tankers caught fire on Thursday and Friday in Tehran’s “prohibited zone” in the Gulf of Oman.
Maritime monitors also reported two tankers struck in Gulf waters off Saudi Arabia on Friday.
Last Sunday, six vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the most in a single day since the war began, according to security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the UK maritime agency UKMTO.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.
Nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through on October 8, but only 2.9 million on October 11, according to Kpler data.
The disruption has pushed up global energy prices and inflation.
US President Donald Trump has explicitly ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran. “I wouldn’t use nuclear,” he told the Newsmax news site in an interview on Thursday.
Trump said that he was also not considering putting troops on the ground in Iran. “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it,” he said, adding he believes a deal to end the war will be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.

articles.title: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means  Al JazeeraIran war updates: Five killed, 16 hurt in Houthi attack on palace in Aden  Al Jazeera2 missiles strike the airport in Yemen's port city of Aden, officials say  The HinduMissiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu  ReutersHouthis hit Yemen airport as Saudi Arabia intercepts attacks  ThePrint
articles.full_text:
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday.
On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo.
Recommended Stories
After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.
The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war, largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?
Here’s what you need to know:
What happened at Maashiq Palace?
The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.
Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.
The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.
What happened at the airport?
On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.
Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.
The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.
Why are attacks on Aden significant?
Aden is the interim capital of Yemen.
The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.
The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.
The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.
But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.
Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
The city has been hit before.
In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.
A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.
What reaction has there been?
On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.
He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.
Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.
Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.
“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.
The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.
What is happening in the wider conflict?
Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.
Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.
The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.
On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.
In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.
Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

articles.title: Ukraine out of stock, allies in a queue, and the US Patriot missiles now shaping wars and alliances | HT Explainers - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: Ukraine out of stock, allies in a queue, and the US Patriot missiles now shaping wars and alliances | HT Explainers  Hindustan TimesExclusive: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles as Zelensky and Trump clash over war  CNNUkraine Out Of US-Made Patriot Interceptors Amid Increased Russian Attacks: Report  NDTVGreece Explained Why It Is Not Providing Patriot Missiles to Ukraine  UA.NEWSUkraine critically low on Patriot interceptors as Russian stri...
articles.full_text:
Ukraine has run out and Gulf allies are hedging, while Poland and Switzerland wait for deliveries. Production will take years to catch up
The shortage of Patriot interceptors in Ukraine is the latest example of how a US-made air-defence system has become one of the main factors steering active wars and pushing governments from Saudi Arabia to Switzerland to rethink where their protection comes from.
Citing a source, CNN reported on Thursday that Ukraine had run out of Patriot interceptors. The Washington Post reported the same day that Kyiv was down to its last Patriot missiles, as Russia continued striking the country's power grid ahead of winter.
Since the US and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, interceptors earmarked for Ukraine have gone to the US military and to US allies in the Gulf, Reuters reported in August. Poland and Switzerland are waiting on the same production line.
And few weapons can take the Patriot's place. "There are no good alternatives to Patriot and THAAD for ballistic missile defence," Mark Cancian and Chris Park of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington think tank, wrote in a report in July. THAAD, a US system that intercepts missiles at higher altitudes, is scarcer still.
Also read: How the Patriot missile system works, and why it's so hard to replace
Ukraine
Overnight into October 14, Russian ballistic missiles hit three power plants in Kyiv and targeted energy infrastructure in Kharkiv, killing four people in Kyiv and injuring 25, CNN reported. The source who spoke to CNN said "almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles".
Speed is the problem. Russia's Iskander short-range ballistic missiles take just a few minutes to reach targets in Ukraine, AP reported. That leaves almost no time to respond without a system built for the task.
The shortfall has been building for months. On August 1, Ukraine shot down only one of the 27 ballistic missiles Russia fired, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had said at the time, according to Reuters. Later that month, he told CNN that Ukraine had a tenth of the interceptors it urgently needed.
The interceptors have also become a lever in a widening feud between Kyiv and Washington. US President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries for record US diesel prices, and has struck a deal to import Russian diesel. The US warned Ukraine and European allies that it could suspend European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, if Ukraine did not halt its deep strikes on Russian energy facilities, CNN reported.
Those purchases run through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), the Nato arrangement through which allies, mostly European, pay for US weapons sent to Ukraine. Patriot shipments are part of this arrangement.
Trump has said the US has not stopped sharing intelligence. Zelenskyy, for his part, told the Financial Times he could agree to halt the energy strikes only if Ukraine received more Patriot interceptors at a "minimum". He has since announced that Ukraine would continue striking Russian refineries.
Kyiv has also tried to make the missiles itself. At a meeting in Ankara in July, Trump said the US would grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture the PAC-3, the newest Patriot interceptor. Within weeks he told reporters the US must be "very careful about letting somebody build them". Zelenskyy later said Trump had told him at their last meeting that he had made a "final decision" in Ukraine's favour, AFP reported. No licence has materialised, according to CNN.
But even with a deal, Ukraine would not receive new missiles for a year or more.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs 5% of the US stock of Patriot interceptors to get through the winter, and 10% to destroy all of Russia's ballistic missiles, according to AFP.
Also read: Pentagon widens Patriot missile order to nearly $59 billion
Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia allocated between $64 billion and $96 billion for defence this year, the upper end being more than twice what Israel spends, and the kingdom operates Patriot batteries with the latest PAC-3 interceptors, Bloomberg reported.
Even so, attacks by the Houthis, the Iran-backed group that controls much of Yemen, hit the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300. It was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing.
Patriot batteries do not cover a full circle, and those positioned to intercept Iranian fire may not have been able to easily stop Houthi missiles, Becca Wasser, who leads defence analysis at Bloomberg Economics, told Bloomberg. Even a layered defence "cannot create an impermeable dome over a country the size of Saudi Arabia", Andreas Krieg of MENA Analytica, a London-based risk firm, told AFP.
Riyadh has asked Washington for more help. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked Trump directly for military assistance after Houthi attacks in early September and was rebuffed, Reuters reported.
The US provides intelligence, target identification and planning for a Saudi-led offensive but has not struck the Houthis itself.
US influence in the region after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 led many governments to rely on US firepower rather than build their own. Saudi Arabia was not immune to this “protection curse”, David Roberts, a reader in international security and Middle East studies at King's College London, told Bloomberg.
But Riyadh has now begun to diversify.
In August, Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Pakistan and Turkey, which the Atlantic Council, a Washington think tank, said was an effort to reduce its dependence on the US, though the pact includes no arms transfers or joint production of munitions.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE's rulers, called for joint Gulf action against attacks by Iran and its allies.
"It has become clear that we are all targeted, and that our security is indivisible," he wrote on social media.
The war showed the need for cheaper counter-drone systems and deeper interceptor reserves, the Stimson Center, another Washington think tank, said in a paper on US bases in the Gulf.
Also read: How are Houthis able to penetrate Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Europe
US allies beyond the war zones are affected too.
“At this point, it looks like we are going to be affected as well. That's very visible in the area of PAC-3 MSE Patriot missiles, they're going to be delayed for sure," Gen Ireneusz Nowak, the Polish army's operational commander, told the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12, Reuters reported.
Switzerland ordered five Patriot systems in 2022, and their delivery had already slipped by four to five years because of the war in Ukraine.
In May, it said the US had warned of further delays because of the Iran war, and that it would look at systems from suppliers in Germany, France, Israel and South Korea, preferably made in Europe. "All options would lead to delivery delays as well as substantial additional costs," the Swiss government said.
Germany, meanwhile, has given about a third of its own Patriot systems to Ukraine, according to the Atlantic Council.
The queue is long because supply is thin. Lockheed Martin makes about 600 PAC-3 MSE interceptors a year and plans to reach 2,000 by 2030, according to CSIS. "Because 18 other countries use the Patriot, these missiles are highly sought after. About half of the annual production goes to support these allies and partners," Cancian and Park wrote in April.
CSIS estimates that the US stock of Patriot interceptors fell from about 2,330 before the Iran war to between 759 and 827 by late July. (Pentagon has pushed back against concerns that its capabilities have diminished).
"China does not need the United States to run out of weapons to exploit the strain," Tressa Guenov, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former senior Pentagon official, and her colleague Bailey Galicia wrote in August.
What’s next?
Expanded production, and the rebuilding of stocks, is years away. For munitions orders of this kind, the time from funding to a completed delivery takes about 52 months, CSIS estimates.
Until then, Washington will decide who goes without. "Until this increased production becomes available, the United States will face choices on allocating production to meet demands," Cancian and Park wrote, adding: "Other US allies are also in the queue."
For now, Ukraine enters winter with almost no Patriot interceptors. Saudi Arabia has signed a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, and Switzerland is weighing suppliers beyond the US.
